On a full English breakfast.Bacon: The traditional rasher is back bacon, which includes a lean loin and a strip of belly, so it is meatier than American streaky strips.
On a full English breakfast.Sausage: Typically a pork banger; the nickname comes from World War I when watery sausages burst with a bang when fried.
On a full English breakfast.Fried egg: Some prefer it sunny-side up with a runny yolk for dipping toast, and the egg is the centerpiece of this plate, which is also called a fry-up.
On a full English breakfast.Baked beans: Haricot beans in tomato sauce are a British breakfast staple, and Heinz introduced them to Britain in 1901.
On a full English breakfast.Black pudding: A sausage of pig's blood, fat and oatmeal or barley; despite the name, it is not a dessert, and has been eaten across Britain for centuries.
On a full English breakfast.Grilled tomato: The tomato half is grilled or fried, adding acidity to cut through the richness of the fry-up, and is one of the few vegetables on the plate.
On a full English breakfast.Mushrooms: Fried button or field mushrooms are a common part of the breakfast, and they absorb the bacon fat they are cooked in.
On a full English breakfast.Toast: Toast is a standard part of the fry-up, usually buttered, and made with white or brown sliced bread, often to mop up the egg yolk and beans.
On a full English breakfast.Fried bread: Bread fried in bacon fat or oil is a classic, though a cholesterol worry has made it a rarer element of the modern café plate.
On a full English breakfast.Pancakes: A trap: pancakes are an American-style breakfast, and a British pancake is thin and crepe-like; they are not on the traditional plate.
On a full English breakfast.Waffles: Waffles are a Belgian and American breakfast and not part of the English one, though they appear on hotel buffets.
On a full English breakfast.Grits: Grits are a Southern United States dish of ground corn, which has no place on a British plate.
On a full English breakfast.Bagel: The bagel is a Jewish breakfast tradition that came to America via Polish immigrants; it is not on the English plate.
On a full English breakfast.Croissant: The croissant belongs to a continental breakfast, a lighter French-style meal, which is the opposite of a full English.
On a full English breakfast.Avocado: Avocado toast is a modern brunch trend, and it never made it onto the traditional full English plate.
On a full English breakfast.Granola: Granola was developed in the US in the 1800s as a health food, and it is not part of a full English.
On a full English breakfast.Biscuits and gravy: A Southern American breakfast of savory scones with sausage gravy; British biscuits are cookies, so the name confuses.
On a full English breakfast.Burrito: A breakfast burrito is a Tex-Mex dish, not part of a traditional English breakfast.
On a full English breakfast.Kimchi: Kimchi is Korean, and has no role in an English breakfast, but it is eaten with morning meals in Korea.
On a full English breakfast.Maple syrup: Maple syrup is for pancakes and waffles; the English breakfast has brown sauce or ketchup instead.
On a full English breakfast.Cereal: Cereal is a separate light breakfast, and a full English is meant to be eaten as the whole meal rather than as an addition to it.
On a full English breakfast.French toast: French toast is not French in origin: Romans had a similar dish, and it is not part of an English breakfast.
On a full English breakfast.Smoothie: A smoothie is a modern health drink, and at odds with the cooked, fatty full English breakfast.
On a full English breakfast.Muesli: Muesli was invented around 1900 by Swiss doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner, and is a cold cereal, not part of the English fry-up.

Japanese drinks.Sake: Japan's rice wine, brewed with koji mold, and with a ceremonial role in Shinto rituals and weddings.
Japanese drinks.Shochu: A distilled Japanese spirit made from barley, sweet potato or rice, often weaker than whisky and drunk with water or hot water.
Japanese drinks.Ramune: A Japanese lemon-lime soda sold in a Codd-neck bottle, where you push a glass marble down to open it.
Japanese drinks.Calpis: A milky, tangy Japanese soft drink made with lactic acid bacteria, which was inspired by Mongolian fermented milk.
Japanese drinks.Sencha: The most common Japanese green tea, from steamed leaves, and a daily staple in homes.
Japanese drinks.Genmaicha: Green tea blended with toasted rice, known as popcorn tea, and it was once a cheaper tea for the poor.
Japanese drinks.Hojicha: Japanese green tea roasted until brown, which gives a toasty, low-caffeine, mellow taste.
Japanese drinks.Umeshu: A sweet Japanese liqueur made by steeping green ume plums in alcohol and sugar.
Japanese drinks.Yakult: A small bottle of probiotic milk drink, developed in the 1930s by Dr Minoru Shirota and sold in more than 40 countries.
Japanese drinks.Matcha: Powdered shade-grown green tea, whisked in the Japanese tea ceremony and used in sweets and ice cream.
Japanese drinks.Pocari Sweat: A Japanese sports drink, with a name that sounds unappetizing but is an electrolyte drink, launched by Otsuka in 1980.
Japanese drinks.Soju: A Korean spirit, which Korea made popular, so not Japanese, though it is sometimes confused with shochu.
Japanese drinks.Makgeolli: A milky Korean rice wine, lightly sparkling and traditionally drunk from a bowl.
Japanese drinks.Baijiu: A strong Chinese grain spirit, including famous brands such as Moutai, and not from Japan.
Japanese drinks.Bubble tea: Invented in Taiwan in the 1980s, so not Japanese, though it is popular in Japan.
Japanese drinks.Lassi: A yogurt-based Indian drink, so not Japanese.
Japanese drinks.Chai: Indian spiced milk tea, and so not Japanese.
Japanese drinks.Mezcal: A Mexican agave spirit, and not Japanese.
Japanese drinks.Pu-erh: A fermented Chinese tea from Yunnan, so not Japanese.
Japanese drinks.Thai iced tea: An orange, sweetened tea with condensed milk, from Thailand.
Japanese drinks.Sikhye: A sweet Korean rice drink with malt, traditionally served after meals, so it isn't Japanese.
Japanese drinks.Yerba mate: A South American holly infusion, not Japanese.
Japanese drinks.Ouzo: A Greek anise spirit that turns cloudy when water is added, and one that has nothing to do with Japanese drinks.
Japanese drinks.Kvass: A Slavic fermented rye bread drink, so not Japanese.

Named winds.Sirocco: This hot, dusty wind rises over the Sahara and rides north across the Mediterranean, sometimes carrying red sand that stains cars in southern Europe.
Named winds.Mistral: A cold, dry wind funneling down the Rhône valley into southern France; it can blow for days and is said to have driven Van Gogh to distraction.
Named winds.Chinook: Called the snow eater, this warm Rocky Mountain wind can lift winter temperatures by 20 degrees Celsius or more within hours.
Named winds.Santa Ana: Hot, dry gusts from the interior blow toward the California coast each autumn and are infamous for fanning wildfires.
Named winds.Foehn: A warm, dry wind that descends the lee side of the Alps; its name has become the general term for this mountain-wind effect worldwide.
Named winds.Harmattan: A dry, dusty West African trade wind that arrives from the Sahara in winter, cracking lips and coating everything in fine haze.
Named winds.Bora: A fierce cold wind blasting down onto the Adriatic coast near Trieste, with gusts strong enough to overturn lorries and close roads.
Named winds.Zephyr: In Greek myth Zephyrus was the god of the gentle west wind, so the word now means any soft, pleasant breeze.
Named winds.Simoom: Its name means poisoning in Arabic. This scorching, sand-laden desert wind can push temperatures past 50 degrees Celsius within minutes.
Named winds.Khamsin: Egyptians named this hot desert wind for the Arabic word for fifty, since it traditionally blows around fifty days in spring.
Named winds.Levanter: An easterly wind funneling through the Strait of Gibraltar; it brings cloud and damp, and can make crossing the strait rough.
Named winds.Tsunami: A trap: a tsunami is a wave, usually from an undersea earthquake, not a wind. The word is Japanese for harbor wave.
Named winds.Aurora: Not a wind: the aurora is light made when charged particles from the solar wind strike gases high in our atmosphere.
Named winds.El Niño: Not a wind, but a warming of Pacific surface waters that shifts weather worldwide. Its name, the Christ child, refers to its Christmastime arrival.
Named winds.Cumulus: A cloud type, not a wind. Those puffy fair-weather clouds can weigh hundreds of tonnes, held aloft by rising warm air.
Named winds.Gulf Stream: A warm ocean current, not a wind, though winds help drive it. It keeps western Europe far milder than other places at similar latitudes.
Named winds.Humboldt Current: A cold ocean current off South America's west coast, not a wind. It feeds one of the planet's richest fisheries, anchovies especially.
Named winds.Equinox: A moment, not a wind: twice a year day and night are nearly equal as the sun crosses the equator.
Named winds.Solstice: A date, not a wind. At the solstice the sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky, giving the longest or shortest day.
Named winds.Doldrums: Sailors dreaded this calm belt near the equator where winds die, though it is a region, not a wind. It also gave us the idiom for a slump.
Named winds.Isobar: A line on a weather map joining points of equal pressure. Isobars packed closely together mean strong winds, but they are not a wind themselves.
Named winds.Tundra: A treeless cold biome, not a wind. Its soil below the surface stays frozen year-round as permafrost.
Named winds.Savanna: A grassland dotted with trees, not a wind. Africa's savannas host the greatest migrations of large mammals on Earth.
Named winds.Fjord: A glacier-carved sea inlet with steep walls, not a wind. Norway's Sognefjord runs over 200 kilometers inland.

Cooking in water or stock or steam.Boiling: At sea level it's 100 degrees Celsius, but at altitude water boils at a lower temperature, so food takes longer to cook.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Poaching: Its gentle 70 to 80 degrees Celsius keeps eggs and fish tender, without the churning of a rolling boil.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Steaming: A bamboo steamer in Chinese cooking keeps food above the water, so flavors and nutrients stay in the food.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Simmering: Just below a boil, with only small bubbles, it's the secret of clear broth and tender stews.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Blanching: A quick dip in boiling water followed by an ice bath fixes the green color of vegetables.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Parboiling: It's a partial boil. Parboiled rice, steamed under pressure before milling, keeps more nutrients and stays firmer when cooked.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Coddling: Traditionally, eggs are lightly cooked in hot water in a small porcelain cup with a lid, just off the heat.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Stewing: Small pieces covered in liquid, unlike a braise, which uses just a bit of liquid.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Braising: You brown the meat first, then cook it slowly in a little liquid in a covered pot, until it falls apart.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Pressure cooking: Denis Papin built his 'steam digester' in 1679, the ancestor of today's pressure cooker, and cooking is faster under pressure.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Roasting: Dry oven heat browns the outside of food. Water is not used, which is why roast potatoes crisp.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Baking: Another dry-heat method, though steam in the oven helps the crust of bread, it isn't cooked in water.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Grilling: Direct heat from below, with no liquid, produces the char and smoky flavor that boiling can't.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Broiling: The heat is from above in a broiler, and dry, quick, and intense, which is the reverse of a gentle simmer.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Searing: Searing browns the surface by the Maillard reaction, but it doesn't actually seal in juices, as the old myth says.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Toasting: A dry method that browns bread by radiant heat, not water.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Smoking: Smoke and low heat cook the food, without any liquid bath.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Sautéing: The name comes from French sauter, 'to jump', since food is tossed in a hot pan with a little fat.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Deep frying: Hot oil, not water, cooks the food, and the surface crisps as the moisture is driven off.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Stir-frying: In a very hot wok, fast stirring cooks food in oil in a few minutes. No simmering liquid is involved.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Barbecuing: In the US, this means slow cooking over smoke, but in Britain it usually means grilling. Neither uses water.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Flambéing: Alcohol is set on fire for flavor and show, but the flames burn off much less alcohol than people think.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Charring: The browning is dry-heat cooking over flame or coals, with no water involved.
Cooking in water or stock or steam.Pan frying: A frying pan with a little fat browns the surface, so it's dry heat, not a moist method.

Things made from grapes.Wine: Fermented grape juice, and one of the oldest crafted drinks. Archaeologists found winemaking traces in Georgia dating back about 8,000 years.
Things made from grapes.Raisins: Sun-dried or machine-dried grapes. Most of the world's supply comes from just a few regions, including California and Turkey.
Things made from grapes.Cognac: Brandy distilled twice from white wine grapes in the Cognac region of France. It must age at least two years in oak.
Things made from grapes.Grappa: Italian spirit distilled from pomace, the skins, seeds and stems left after winemaking. It makes use of what would be waste.
Things made from grapes.Balsamic vinegar: Traditional versions are boiled grape must aged for at least 12 years in a series of wooden barrels in Modena.
Things made from grapes.Champagne: Sparkling wine that legally comes only from the Champagne region of France. The bubbles come from a second fermentation inside the bottle.
Things made from grapes.Port: A sweet wine from Portugal's Douro Valley, fortified with grape spirit partway through fermentation to keep the sugar.
Things made from grapes.Sherry: Fortified wine from southern Spain, made around Jerez. It is aged in a stacked solera system that blends old and young vintages.
Things made from grapes.Pisco: Grape brandy claimed by both Peru and Chile as their national spirit. It is the base of the pisco sour.
Things made from grapes.Sultanas: Dried pale grapes, usually from seedless varieties. They are a classic ingredient in British fruit cake and scones.
Things made from grapes.Vermouth: White wine fortified and flavored with herbs and botanicals, including wormwood. The name comes from the German word for wormwood.
Things made from grapes.Grape jelly: Made from grape juice, sugar and pectin. Paired with peanut butter, it became an American lunchbox classic.
Things made from grapes.Prosecco: Italian sparkling wine made mainly from the Glera grape. Most is made in tanks rather than bottles, which keeps it fruity and cheaper.
Things made from grapes.Cider: Made from fermented apple juice, not grapes. In much of Europe, it has been brewed since medieval times.
Things made from grapes.Perry: Fermented pear juice, the pear cousin of cider. The classic English version comes from perry pear trees that can live centuries.
Things made from grapes.Mead: Fermented honey, with no grapes involved. It is among the oldest alcoholic drinks in history, and Vikings loved it.
Things made from grapes.Sake: Brewed from rice, not grapes. Despite being called rice wine, the brewing process is closer to beer.
Things made from grapes.Calvados: Apple brandy from Normandy. It is made from cider apples and sometimes pears, then aged in oak.
Things made from grapes.Kirsch: Clear cherry brandy distilled from the fruit and its stones. It is the key to Swiss cheese fondue and Black Forest cake.
Things made from grapes.Slivovitz: Plum brandy from the Balkans, a treasured national drink in Serbia. It is made from fermented plums.
Things made from grapes.Rum: Made from sugarcane juice or molasses, not grapes. It was the drink of the Caribbean and British navy sailors.
Things made from grapes.Tequila: Distilled from the blue agave plant, which takes about eight years to mature. Not all agave spirits qualify as tequila.
Things made from grapes.Whisky: Distilled from fermented grain mash such as barley, corn or rye. Scotch must be aged at least three years.
Things made from grapes.Prunes: Dried plums, not grapes, though many people mix them up with raisins. Prunes are higher in fiber and sorbitol.

Cities in Brazil.Rio de Janeiro: Rio's Christ the Redeemer statue stands about 30 meters tall atop Corcovado, and the city hosts the world's biggest Carnival.
Cities in Brazil.São Paulo: São Paulo is the biggest city in the Southern Hemisphere, with more than 12 million people, and has the largest Japanese community outside Japan.
Cities in Brazil.Brasília: Brasília was built from scratch in the late 1950s and made the capital in 1960, and its layout from above resembles an airplane.
Cities in Brazil.Salvador: Salvador was Brazil's first capital, and is the heart of Afro-Brazilian culture, where capoeira and acarajé thrive.
Cities in Brazil.Recife: Recife is called the Venice of Brazil for its rivers and bridges, and it has a lively frevo music scene at Carnival.
Cities in Brazil.Manaus: Manaus sits in the Amazon rainforest, and its grand opera house was built in the rubber boom of the 1890s.
Cities in Brazil.Fortaleza: Fortaleza is a beach city on the northeast coast, where the sun shines most of the year.
Cities in Brazil.Belo Horizonte: Belo Horizonte's name means beautiful horizon, and it is known for its many bars and cheese bread, pão de queijo.
Cities in Brazil.Curitiba: Curitiba is famous for its bus rapid transit system, which inspired systems around the world.
Cities in Brazil.Porto Alegre: Porto Alegre is the capital of Rio Grande do Sul, where gaúcho cowboys grill meat in churrasco.
Cities in Brazil.Buenos Aires: Buenos Aires is the capital of Argentina, where the tango was born, not in Brazil.
Cities in Brazil.Lima: Lima is the capital of Peru, and is one of the driest capitals in the world, almost without rain.
Cities in Brazil.Bogotá: Bogotá is Colombia's capital, at about 2,600 meters, one of the highest capitals in the world.
Cities in Brazil.Montevideo: Montevideo is the capital of Uruguay, and it's home to nearly half of the country's people.
Cities in Brazil.Lisbon: Lisbon is Portugal's capital, and its link to Brazil goes back to the colonial days.
Cities in Brazil.Porto: Porto is a Portuguese city, though Brazil shares the Portuguese language and the city's name appears in several Brazilian towns.
Cities in Brazil.Asunción: Asunción is the capital of Paraguay, one of the oldest cities in South America, founded in 1537.
Cities in Brazil.Santiago: Santiago is the capital of Chile, set between the Andes and a coastal range.
Cities in Brazil.Caracas: Caracas is the capital of Venezuela, and sits in a valley under El Ávila mountain.
Cities in Brazil.La Paz: La Paz is Bolivia's seat of government, and the highest in the world, at around 3,600 meters.
Cities in Brazil.Cusco: Cusco is in Peru and was the Inca capital, near Machu Picchu.
Cities in Brazil.Quito: Quito is Ecuador's capital, and sits very close to the equator, and has a UNESCO-listed old town.
Cities in Brazil.Rosario: Rosario is an Argentine city, birthplace of Che Guevara and Lionel Messi.
Cities in Brazil.Luanda: Luanda is the capital of Angola, and was a Portuguese colony city, like many in Brazil, but it lies in Africa.

Flags with a star.USA: The 50th star was added for Hawaii in 1959. The 50-star design has outlasted every earlier version, now flying unchanged for over six decades.
Flags with a star.China: The big star on the red flag stands for the Communist Party, and the four smaller ones for the social classes. The red field stands for revolution.
Flags with a star.Vietnam: The single yellow star on a red field has five points, said to stand for workers, farmers, soldiers, intellectuals and youth.
Flags with a star.Brazil: The blue disc shows the actual night sky over Rio on the day the republic was declared in 1889, with 27 stars for its states and capital.
Flags with a star.Australia: Its flag shows the Southern Cross constellation and a large Commonwealth Star with seven points, one for each state plus the territories.
Flags with a star.New Zealand: Four red stars with white borders form the Southern Cross. The country held two referendums on changing the flag, in 2015 and 2016, and kept it.
Flags with a star.Turkey: The white crescent and star on red is a famous design. Some say it echoes the moon's reflection on blood after a battle, a legend rather than history.
Flags with a star.Chile: A single white star on a blue square, and the star stands for a guide to progress and honor. Its flag looks a lot like Texas's, which has a similar layout.
Flags with a star.Cuba: The white star on a red triangle is called the lone star. The flag was designed in the 1840s, with its three blue stripes for the island's old regions.
Flags with a star.Ghana: Its black star is the lone star of African freedom. Ghana was the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence, in 1957, and the star inspired others.
Flags with a star.Somalia: The white star on pale blue was designed in 1954 and points out the five regions where Somalis live. The sky blue shade echoes the United Nations flag.
Flags with a star.Pakistan: The white crescent and star sit on a green field, with a white stripe at the hoist for minorities. The star stands for light and knowledge.
Flags with a star.Philippines: The sun in its triangle has eight rays for the first provinces to rebel against Spain, and three stars for Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao.
Flags with a star.Canada: The 11-point red maple leaf is the only emblem here, not a star. The flag was adopted in 1965 after years of fierce debate in parliament.
Flags with a star.Japan: A red disc on white has no star, and it's named the Nisshoki or Hinomaru. Its simple form has been used for centuries as the symbol of the sun.
Flags with a star.France: The tricolor has three plain vertical bands in blue, white and red, with no star. The bands trace back to the 1789 revolution.
Flags with a star.Germany: The black, red and gold horizontal bands have no star. The colors date back to a 19th-century liberal movement.
Flags with a star.Italy: The tricolor in green, white and red has no star. It was inspired by the French flag brought by Napoleon's armies in the 1790s.
Flags with a star.UK: The Union Jack combines three crosses and has no stars. It layers the crosses of St. George, St. Andrew and St. Patrick.
Flags with a star.India: The flag has a blue 24-spoke wheel, the Ashoka Chakra, at its center. It's a wheel and not a star.
Flags with a star.South Korea: The Taegukgi uses a red and blue yin-yang circle and four black trigrams, with no star. The trigrams stand for heaven, earth, fire and water.
Flags with a star.Mexico: The flag carries an eagle perched on a cactus, devouring a snake, with no star. It's based on an Aztec legend about the founding of Tenochtitlan.
Flags with a star.Argentina: The Sun of May is at the center of its sky-blue and white stripes. It's a sun with a face, not a star.
Flags with a star.Sweden: A yellow Nordic cross on blue, and no star in sight. The colors come from the national coat of arms, with three golden crowns on blue.

Countries that are monarchies.UK: King Charles III is head of state of 15 countries, the UK among them. Its monarchy has run, with interruptions, for over a thousand years.
Countries that are monarchies.Spain: The monarchy was restored in 1975 after Franco's death, and King Juan Carlos helped steer the country to democracy.
Countries that are monarchies.Sweden: Its king has no political power; since a 1980 reform the crown goes to the eldest child regardless of sex, first applying to Princess Victoria.
Countries that are monarchies.Norway: A constitutional monarchy since independence from Sweden in 1905, when the people voted to choose a Danish prince as king.
Countries that are monarchies.Denmark: One of the world's oldest monarchies, its royal line stretches back over a thousand years, to Gorm the Old.
Countries that are monarchies.Netherlands: Its royal house is Orange-Nassau, and the national colour orange comes from it, celebrated on King's Day each April.
Countries that are monarchies.Belgium: Founded as a kingdom in 1830, it has a king though the country had no government for a record 541 days in 2010 to 2011.
Countries that are monarchies.Japan: Has the world's oldest continuous hereditary monarchy, and its emperor is the only one left on Earth.
Countries that are monarchies.Thailand: The king is deeply revered, and insulting him is a crime under strict laws; the royal line goes back to the Chakri dynasty of 1782.
Countries that are monarchies.Morocco: The king holds real power, and his family claims descent from the Prophet Muhammad, which gives it religious standing too.
Countries that are monarchies.Jordan: A kingdom ruled by the Hashemite dynasty, which claims descent from the Prophet Muhammad, with King Abdullah II on the throne since 1999.
Countries that are monarchies.Monaco: A principality ruled by the Grimaldi family since 1297, it's the second-smallest country on Earth after the Vatican.
Countries that are monarchies.France: A republic since the Revolution; it executed Louis XVI in 1793 and has had no king in power since 1848.
Countries that are monarchies.Germany: A federal republic. Its last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, abdicated in 1918 at the end of World War I.
Countries that are monarchies.Italy: Voted in 1946 to abolish the monarchy by about 54 percent, in a referendum women could vote in for the first time nationally.
Countries that are monarchies.Greece: Its monarchy ended after a 1974 referendum, which followed years of a military junta, and the former king was never restored.
Countries that are monarchies.Russia: A republic since the 1917 revolution ended the tsars; Nicholas II and his family were executed in 1918.
Countries that are monarchies.Portugal: Became a republic in 1910 after a revolution deposed its last king, Manuel II, who fled to England.
Countries that are monarchies.Ireland: A republic, though in 1949 it formally left the British Commonwealth and cut the last ties to the crown.
Countries that are monarchies.Finland: A republic since 1919, even though a 1918 attempt to crown a German prince as its king never came to be.
Countries that are monarchies.Austria: A republic since 1918, when the Habsburg empire, which ruled for centuries, collapsed.
Countries that are monarchies.India: A republic since 1950. Its former princely states, ruled by maharajas, were absorbed after independence.
Countries that are monarchies.Iran: A republic since the 1979 revolution, which overthrew the last shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
Countries that are monarchies.Egypt: A republic since 1953, when it abolished the monarchy after the 1952 coup that ended the line of King Farouk.

Famous streets of New York City.Broadway: This street runs the length of Manhattan, roughly 21 kilometres, and began as a Native American trail; its theatre district gave the world its name for musicals.
Famous streets of New York City.Fifth Avenue: Divides Manhattan's east and west addresses and has long been one of the world's priciest shopping streets, home to Tiffany and Saks.
Famous streets of New York City.Wall Street: Named after a wall built by Dutch settlers in the 1600s, this short street houses the New York Stock Exchange.
Famous streets of New York City.Park Avenue: Once lined with railway tracks that ran above ground, it's now a boulevard of corporate towers and luxury apartments.
Famous streets of New York City.Madison Avenue: Its name became shorthand for the US advertising industry, which thrived there in the mid-20th century, as Mad Men showed.
Famous streets of New York City.Delancey Street: A major Lower East Side street leading to the Williamsburg Bridge and once the centre of Jewish immigrant life.
Famous streets of New York City.Bleecker Street: A Greenwich Village street long tied to folk music, Bob Dylan, and cult shops and jazz clubs.
Famous streets of New York City.Lexington Avenue: Runs on Manhattan's east side, and its 4, 5 and 6 subway line is one of the busiest in the US.
Famous streets of New York City.Bowery: Once New York's skid row, it's now home to galleries and CBGB, the punk club that launched the Ramones.
Famous streets of New York City.Houston Street: Pronounced HOW-ston in New York, not like the Texas city, and it marks the south end of Greenwich Village.
Famous streets of New York City.Rodeo Drive: Beverly Hills' glamorous luxury shopping street is in California and appears in Pretty Woman.
Famous streets of New York City.Sunset Boulevard: A Los Angeles road about 35 kilometres long, famed for the Sunset Strip and a 1950 film.
Famous streets of New York City.Hollywood Boulevard: Los Angeles's street of the Walk of Fame, with more than 2,600 stars embedded in the pavement.
Famous streets of New York City.Bourbon Street: New Orleans's famous French Quarter street takes its name from a French royal house, not the whiskey.
Famous streets of New York City.Michigan Avenue: Chicago's grand boulevard, whose Magnificent Mile is lined with shops and the Tribune Tower.
Famous streets of New York City.Lombard Street: San Francisco's famously crooked street, with eight hairpin turns on a steep hill.
Famous streets of New York City.Beale Street: Memphis's blues street, where B.B. King and W.C. Handy played, and it's called the home of the blues.
Famous streets of New York City.Magnificent Mile: A section of Michigan Avenue in Chicago filled with shops, not New York.
Famous streets of New York City.Abbey Road: A London street made world famous by the Beatles' 1969 album cover and its crossing.
Famous streets of New York City.Oxford Street: London's main shopping street is Europe's busiest, drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors a day.
Famous streets of New York City.Champs-Élysées: Paris's grand avenue stretches from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe, the finish of the Tour de France.
Famous streets of New York City.Las Vegas Strip: A roughly 6.8-kilometre stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard, mostly outside Las Vegas city limits.
Famous streets of New York City.Haight Street: San Francisco's street at the heart of the 1967 Summer of Love, a hippie hub.
Famous streets of New York City.Ocean Drive: Miami Beach's Art Deco strip, lined with pastel hotels and neon, in Florida.

Laboratory glassware.Beaker: The beaker's markings are only approximate, so precision work uses a graduated cylinder or volumetric flask instead.
Laboratory glassware.Test tube: Test tubes hold small samples and can be heated directly, and many are made of heat-resistant borosilicate glass.
Laboratory glassware.Erlenmeyer flask: Named for German chemist Emil Erlenmeyer in 1860, its conical shape lets you swirl a liquid without spilling.
Laboratory glassware.Florence flask: A round-bodied boiling flask with a long neck, named for the Florentine wine flasks it resembles, but it stands on a flat base.
Laboratory glassware.Burette: A burette is a long graduated tube with a stopcock for dripping exact amounts of liquid during a titration.
Laboratory glassware.Graduated cylinder: Read it at the bottom of the meniscus, the curved liquid surface, for an accurate measurement.
Laboratory glassware.Watch glass: Named for old pocket-watch crystals, this shallow dish serves as a lid, or to evaporate small samples.
Laboratory glassware.Volumetric flask: A volumetric flask is calibrated for one exact volume at one set temperature, usually 20 degrees Celsius.
Laboratory glassware.Round-bottom flask: A round-bottom flask spreads stress evenly, so it withstands heat and vacuum, but needs a ring to stand upright.
Laboratory glassware.Condenser: The Liebig condenser is named for Justus von Liebig, who popularized it though he didn't invent it.
Laboratory glassware.Separatory funnel: This pear-shaped glass funnel separates liquids that don't mix, such as oil and water, by draining the lower layer.
Laboratory glassware.Bunsen burner: A trap: a Bunsen burner is a metal gas burner, and its heat is what the glassware sits above, not glassware itself.
Laboratory glassware.Tongs: A trap: tongs are metal, used to grab hot beakers and crucibles, but they aren't glassware themselves.
Laboratory glassware.Ring stand: A trap: the ring stand is a metal support for holding flasks and clamps above a burner, not glass.
Laboratory glassware.Spatula: A trap: a spatula is a small metal or plastic scoop for powders, so it's a tool, not glassware.
Laboratory glassware.Microscope: A trap: microscopes contain glass lenses and slides, but the microscope itself is an instrument, not glassware.
Laboratory glassware.Centrifuge: A trap: a centrifuge is a motorized machine that spins tubes, so the tubes are glassware but the machine is not.
Laboratory glassware.Scale: A trap: a lab balance weighs samples to tiny fractions of a gram, and is equipment rather than glassware.
Laboratory glassware.Hot plate: A trap: a hot plate heats flasks without a flame, and it's electrical equipment, not glassware.
Laboratory glassware.Goggles: A trap: goggles are protective gear made of plastic, so they fit a lab but not the glassware category.
Laboratory glassware.Clamp: A trap: a clamp is a metal holder that grips glass, not glassware itself.
Laboratory glassware.Mortar and pestle: A trap: a mortar and pestle is usually porcelain or stone, used for grinding, so it's not glassware.
Laboratory glassware.Wire gauze: A trap: wire gauze is a metal mesh with a ceramic center that spreads heat under flasks, not glass.
Laboratory glassware.Lab coat: A trap: a lab coat protects clothing from spills, which makes it safety clothing, not glassware.

Rockets (launch vehicles).Saturn V: The 110-meter rocket that sent Apollo crews to the Moon in 1968 to 1972 never lost a crew, and for decades it was the most powerful rocket ever flown.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Falcon 9: SpaceX's workhorse is the first orbital-class rocket whose first stage routinely lands and flies again, with dozens of reuses on a single booster.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Falcon Heavy: With 27 engines on three boosters, it is among the most powerful rockets flying, and its 2018 debut launched a Tesla Roadster toward Mars orbit.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Soyuz: The Russian family has launched people since 1967, and its design lineage goes back to Sputnik's launcher, making it among the most flown rockets ever.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Ariane 5: Europe's workhorse of 1996 to 2023 launched the James Webb Space Telescope in 2021 so precisely that it saved fuel for years.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Atlas V: A United States rocket with Russian-built engines, which has launched Mars rovers and many national security satellites.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Delta IV: This heavy-lift rocket was the last to carry a Delta name, and it retired in 2024 after launching satellites and the Orion test.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Electron: Rocket Lab's small launcher, built in New Zealand, uses 3D-printed engines and has tried catching boosters with helicopters.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Long March: China's rocket family is named for a famous marching trek, and it is among the most prolific in launches.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Space Launch System: NASA's rocket for Artemis, which flew its first mission around the Moon in 2022 and is the most powerful rocket NASA has built since Saturn V.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Redstone: The early 1950s US Army rocket that launched Alan Shepard on the first American spaceflight in 1961.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Hubble: A space telescope, not a rocket, and it was carried to orbit aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery in 1990.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Voyager 1: It's a probe, not a rocket: launched in 1977 on a Titan rocket, and it's now in interstellar space.
Rockets (launch vehicles).ISS: The space station is a laboratory, not a launcher, and it has orbited Earth since 1998.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Skylab: A space station, not a rocket, and it was launched on a Saturn V in 1973, using the rocket's upper stage.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Sputnik 1: A satellite and not a rocket, and it was launched on a modified R-7 missile in 1957.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Curiosity: The rover is a vehicle that rides on rockets, not a rocket itself, and it landed on Mars in 2012 with a sky crane.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Cassini: A probe that was launched by a Titan IV rocket and studied Saturn, not a launcher.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Mir: A Russian space station that was assembled in orbit from 1986, so it's a payload.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Tiangong: China's space station, a payload launched on Long March rockets, not a rocket.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Juno: A spacecraft that reached Jupiter in 2016 and was carried by an Atlas V, so it is a payload.
Rockets (launch vehicles).New Horizons: It's a probe launched in 2006 by an Atlas V and it's a payload.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Perseverance: A rover that landed on Mars in 2021, carried by an Atlas V rocket, so it's cargo.
Rockets (launch vehicles).Pioneer 10: A probe, the first to Jupiter, was launched on an Atlas rocket and is not a rocket itself.

Types of star.Red dwarf: The most common stars in the galaxy; they burn fuel so slowly they can shine for trillions of years.
Types of star.White dwarf: The leftover core of a Sun-like star, squeezing roughly the Sun's mass into a ball about Earth's size.
Types of star.Red giant: The Sun will become one in about five billion years, swelling enough to swallow Mercury and Venus.
Types of star.Neutron star: A city-sized ball of neutrons whose single teaspoon would weigh billions of tonnes.
Types of star.Red supergiant: Betelgeuse in Orion is one; swap it for the Sun and its surface would reach out past Mars.
Types of star.Pulsar: A spinning neutron star that sweeps beams like a lighthouse; the first, found in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell, was nicknamed LGM for 'little green men'.
Types of star.Yellow dwarf: The Sun is one, and it looks white, not yellow; the yellow tint comes from our atmosphere.
Types of star.Blue giant: Hot, massive and bright, they burn out in just millions of years, a blink compared with the Sun.
Types of star.Magnetar: A neutron star with a magnetic field trillions of times stronger than Earth's, and it can unleash giant flares.
Types of star.Hypergiant: The rarest, most luminous stars, some shining a million times brighter than the Sun.
Types of star.Blue supergiant: Rigel in Orion is one, shining with around 100,000 times the Sun's luminosity.
Types of star.Black hole: A trap: a black hole is what remains after the biggest stars die, with no fusion and no shine, so it is a remnant, not a star.
Types of star.Quasar: An immensely bright galaxy core powered by a supermassive black hole, and it can outshine its entire galaxy.
Types of star.Nebula: A cloud of gas and dust, either a nursery for new stars or a remnant of dead ones; the Orion Nebula is visible by eye.
Types of star.Comet: An icy body that grows a tail near the Sun, but it has no fusion and shines by reflected light.
Types of star.Asteroid: Rocky leftovers from the Solar System's birth, mostly in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.
Types of star.Galaxy: A galaxy holds billions of stars, and the Milky Way has several hundred billion.
Types of star.Shooting star: It is no star at all: a meteor, usually a grain no bigger than sand, burning up in the air.
Types of star.Starfish: A sea star has no brain and no blood, using seawater to power its tube feet.
Types of star.Gas giant: Jupiter is a gas giant, and it would need about 80 times more mass to ignite hydrogen fusion and become a star.
Types of star.Dwarf planet: A trap: Pluto and its kin are called dwarf planets, but a dwarf planet is not a dwarf star; Pluto was reclassified in 2006.
Types of star.Supernova: A star's explosive death rather than a kind of star, and one can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.
Types of star.Moon: It shines by reflecting sunlight, with no fusion of its own.
Types of star.Starfruit: Also called carambola; slices form a five-pointed star, and it is dangerous to people with kidney problems.

Contagious illnesses.Common cold: More than 200 viruses cause the common cold, which is why no single vaccine can stop it and you can catch it again and again.
Contagious illnesses.Flu: Flu viruses mutate quickly, so the vaccine is updated every year. The 1918 pandemic killed tens of millions.
Contagious illnesses.Chickenpox: Chickenpox is highly contagious, and the virus then hides in nerves and can return decades later as shingles.
Contagious illnesses.Measles: Measles is among the most contagious diseases known: one case can infect about 12 to 18 unvaccinated people.
Contagious illnesses.Cold sores: Cold sores come from the herpes simplex virus, which stays in the body for life and flares up under stress or sun.
Contagious illnesses.Head lice: Head lice spread by direct contact and have nothing to do with being dirty. They actually prefer clean hair.
Contagious illnesses.Ringworm: Ringworm has no worm at all. It is a fungal skin infection that gets its name from the circular rash.
Contagious illnesses.Strep throat: Strep throat is caused by bacteria and spreads in droplets. Unlike most sore throats, it needs antibiotics.
Contagious illnesses.Mumps: Mumps swells the cheeks by infecting salivary glands. It was once common in children and is now rare, thanks to vaccines.
Contagious illnesses.Whooping cough: Whooping cough gets its name from the 'whoop' sound of gasping breaths. It is especially dangerous for babies.
Contagious illnesses.COVID-19: COVID-19 spread worldwide from late 2019 and has been responsible for millions of deaths. Vaccines were developed in under a year.
Contagious illnesses.Diabetes: Diabetes is not catchable. Type 1 is an autoimmune problem and type 2 is tied to metabolism and genes.
Contagious illnesses.Asthma: Asthma is a chronic condition, so you can't catch it from others, though infections can trigger attacks.
Contagious illnesses.Allergies: Allergies are an overreaction of the immune system to harmless things. You cannot catch them from another person.
Contagious illnesses.Sunburn: Sunburn is damage from ultraviolet light, not an infection, and no one can catch it from you.
Contagious illnesses.Broken leg: A broken leg is an injury, not an infection, so it cannot be caught, though the cast may collect many signatures.
Contagious illnesses.Appendicitis: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix. It strikes individuals and can't spread to others.
Contagious illnesses.Freckles: Freckles are clusters of pigment, triggered by sun and set by genes. They can't be passed on by contact.
Contagious illnesses.Migraine: A migraine is a neurological condition, far more than a headache, and it is not contagious.
Contagious illnesses.Hay fever: Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen, so you cannot catch it, despite sneezing like a cold.
Contagious illnesses.Arthritis: Arthritis is joint inflammation or wear and tear, with over 100 types. None of them can be caught from another person.
Contagious illnesses.Scurvy: Scurvy comes from a lack of vitamin C and was the sailor's curse. It is not contagious, since it's a deficiency.
Contagious illnesses.Hiccups: Hiccups may feel like they spread when someone nearby has them, but they are not contagious.
Contagious illnesses.Color blindness: Color blindness is usually inherited, affecting about 1 in 12 men and far fewer women, and cannot be caught.

Characters in Zootopia.Roger Rabbit: The star of the 1988 film Who Framed Roger Rabbit shares a city with humans, so he's not a Zootopian.
Characters in Zootopia.Basil: Basil of Baker Street, the mouse sleuth of Disney's The Great Mouse Detective, is modeled on Sherlock Holmes.
Characters in Zootopia.Rocket: The raccoon from Guardians of the Galaxy is a space adventurer, not a Zootopia citizen.
Characters in Zootopia.Buster Moon: The koala theater owner from Sing lives in a different animal city, and not Zootopia.
Characters in Zootopia.Bolt: The superdog of Disney's 2008 film Bolt, who believes his TV powers are real, lives in our world, not Zootopia.

Dances from Latin America.Salsa: The word means sauce. The style blends Cuban rhythms with New York sounds and boomed in 1970s Latin clubs.
Dances from Latin America.Tango: It is from Argentina and Uruguay, and UNESCO added it to its heritage list in 2009.
Dances from Latin America.Samba: Brazil's national rhythm, tied to Rio's Carnival, where huge samba schools parade through the Sambadrome.
Dances from Latin America.Merengue: The Dominican Republic's national dance, with a stiff-legged step that legend says imitates a limping soldier.
Dances from Latin America.Bachata: Born in the Dominican countryside, it was once looked down on as low-class music and later gained UNESCO recognition in 2019.
Dances from Latin America.Rumba: Cuban rumba is a lively street dance with drumming, quite unlike the slow ballroom version.
Dances from Latin America.Cha-cha: Created in Cuba in the 1950s by violinist Enrique Jorrín, it is named for the sound of dancers' shuffling feet.
Dances from Latin America.Mambo: Cuban in origin, it was made famous by Pérez Prado, the King of Mambo, with his 1949 hit Mambo No. 5.
Dances from Latin America.Lambada: This Brazilian dance, nicknamed the forbidden dance, took Europe by storm in 1989.
Dances from Latin America.Cumbia: Colombia's blend of African, Indigenous and Spanish traditions, now popular across all of Latin America.
Dances from Latin America.Conga: A Cuban carnival line dance named for the conga drum that drives it. Miami's 1988 street conga set a record with over 119,000 people.
Dances from Latin America.Flamenco: A Spanish dance from Andalusia, not Latin American, though Spanish-speaking, which makes it a trap.
Dances from Latin America.Polka: A lively dance from Bohemia in the 1830s that swept Europe, so Central European and not Latin American.
Dances from Latin America.Waltz: Born in Austria and southern Germany, so European, though it's now danced in every Latin American ballroom too.
Dances from Latin America.Foxtrot: Developed in the US around 1914, often credited to vaudeville star Harry Fox, so not Latin American.
Dances from Latin America.Hula: Hawaiian, not Latin American. Its hand gestures tell stories, and missionaries tried to suppress it in the 1800s.
Dances from Latin America.Haka: A Maori war dance from New Zealand, best known as the pre-match challenge by the All Blacks rugby team.
Dances from Latin America.Can-can: French, born in Paris cabarets in the 1830s, and once so scandalous the police tried to restrain it.
Dances from Latin America.Jig: A quick Irish or Scottish dance in compound time, so not Latin American, even though Latin America has its own folk traditions.
Dances from Latin America.Quickstep: An English ballroom dance from the 1920s, mixing fast foxtrot with Charleston steps, so not Latin American.
Dances from Latin America.Charleston: Named for Charleston, South Carolina, and the signature dance of the Roaring Twenties.
Dances from Latin America.Lindy hop: Born in Harlem in the 1920s, and named after Charles Lindbergh's transatlantic flight.
Dances from Latin America.Tarantella: From southern Italy, folk tradition says it cured a spider bite by dancing the poison away.
Dances from Latin America.Morris dance: English folk dancing with bells, sticks and handkerchiefs, which has roots stretching back centuries.
