Parts of a guitar.Fretboard: The fretboard is also called the fingerboard; its marked dots, usually at frets 3, 5, 7 and 9, help players find their place.
Parts of a guitar.Neck: A guitar's neck often contains a steel rod, the truss rod, which players adjust to keep it from bowing under string tension.
Parts of a guitar.Headstock: The headstock's shape is a brand signature; Gibson and Fender guitars are recognizable from it alone.
Parts of a guitar.Bridge: On an acoustic guitar the bridge passes string vibrations into the top, so even small changes to it alter the tone.
Parts of a guitar.Pickup: Electric guitar pickups turn string vibration into electricity using magnets and thousands of turns of fine copper wire.
Parts of a guitar.Tuning peg: Tuning pegs are geared, so a full turn changes the string's pitch only a little, making fine tuning easy.
Parts of a guitar.Sound hole: The sound hole mostly lets the air in the body move with the top; it does not simply let sound out.
Parts of a guitar.Nut: The nut is the small slotted piece at the top of the neck that spaces the strings and sets their height.
Parts of a guitar.Saddle: The saddle sits in the bridge and is the point where each string actually ends, so it helps set the guitar's intonation.
Parts of a guitar.Frets: Frets are spaced by a mathematical rule: each is about 5.6 percent closer than the last, giving a note a half step apart.
Parts of a guitar.Strings: Most guitars have six strings, but twelve-string versions double each one so the notes ring with a shimmer.
Parts of a guitar.Reed: Trap: a reed is a thin strip of cane in clarinets and saxophones; a guitar has none.
Parts of a guitar.Valve: Trap: valves belong to brass instruments like the trumpet, where they redirect air through extra tubing.
Parts of a guitar.Mouthpiece: Trap: a mouthpiece is for blown instruments, where it shapes how the player's breath starts the sound.
Parts of a guitar.Bellows: Trap: bellows push air through accordions and bagpipes, but a guitar makes sound by plucked strings.
Parts of a guitar.Drumhead: Trap: the drumhead is the skin you hit on a drum, not part of a guitar.
Parts of a guitar.Mallet: Trap: mallets strike xylophones, timpani and other percussion; guitarists use fingers or picks.
Parts of a guitar.Spit valve: Trap: the spit valve lets condensation drain from brass instruments, which a guitar doesn't have.
Parts of a guitar.Chanter: Trap: the chanter is the melody pipe of the bagpipes, not a guitar part.
Parts of a guitar.Bow: Trap: a bow is for violins and cellos; guitars are plucked or strummed, though some experimental players use bows.
Parts of a guitar.Bell: Trap: the bell is the flared end of a trumpet or clarinet, where sound leaves the instrument.
Parts of a guitar.Hi-hat: Trap: the hi-hat is a pair of cymbals on a stand in a drum kit.
Parts of a guitar.Damper pedal: Trap: the damper pedal is a piano's sustain pedal, which lifts felt dampers off the strings.
Parts of a guitar.Rosin: Trap: rosin is a sticky tree resin rubbed on violin bows to grip the strings, so it belongs to bowed instruments.

Boxing terms.Jab: A jab is a quick, straight punch with the lead hand, and it is the foundation of boxing since it keeps opponents at range.
Boxing terms.Uppercut: An uppercut is thrown upward from low position, aiming for the chin, and it can end a fight with a single hit.
Boxing terms.Hook: A hook is a looping punch with a bent arm that targets the head or body from the side.
Boxing terms.Knockout: A knockout occurs when a fighter can't rise by a ten count, and boxers can score one even from a single punch.
Boxing terms.Southpaw: A southpaw is a left-handed boxer who leads with the right hand, and the name may come from baseball pitchers whose left arm was on the south side.
Boxing terms.Clinch: A clinch is a hold that ties up the opponent's arms, which stops them from punching and lets the fighters rest.
Boxing terms.Haymaker: A haymaker is a wild, swinging punch thrown with all the strength, and its name comes from swinging a scythe at hay.
Boxing terms.Cross: A cross is a straight punch thrown with the rear hand across the body, and it is a power shot in a one-two combination.
Boxing terms.Bob and weave: Bob and weave is the head movement that ducks under punches by sinking and moving side to side.
Boxing terms.Standing count: A standing count gives a referee a chance to count to eight for a stunned boxer who is still on his feet.
Boxing terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is basketball's; boxing's big finish is a knockout.
Boxing terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is football's; in boxing, the goal of the ring is to put an opponent down.
Boxing terms.Home run: A home run is baseball's; boxing's nearest is a big right hand.
Boxing terms.Birdie: A birdie is golf's; in boxing, the lightest classes are called bantamweight, a bird-named division.
Boxing terms.Wicket: A wicket is cricket's; a boxing ring is 16 to 20 feet square, though it is called a ring.
Boxing terms.Checkmate: Checkmate is chess; boxing's nearest is a fighter being cornered on the ropes.
Boxing terms.Scrum: A scrum is rugby's; boxing's contact is limited to the gloves and the clinch.
Boxing terms.Love: Love is tennis's zero; boxing's nearest is the scorecard, in which a round can be scored 10-8 for a knockdown.
Boxing terms.Puck: A puck is hockey's; boxing's equipment is gloves, typically 8 to 10 ounces for most pro fights.
Boxing terms.Icing: Icing is hockey's, and the boxer's ice is a cold compress on the eye.
Boxing terms.Gutter ball: A gutter ball is bowling's; a boxer's nearest is a punch that misses and hits only air.
Boxing terms.Free kick: A free kick is soccer's; boxing's equivalent is a foul called for hitting below the belt.
Boxing terms.Spare: A spare is bowling's; boxing's cornermen are also called seconds, who patch fighters between rounds.
Boxing terms.Googly: A googly is cricket's; boxing's feints, like the shoulder shrug, act as a trick.

Winter Olympics stars.Shaun White: The Flying Tomato won three Olympic golds in the snowboard halfpipe, and his 2010 run included the Double McTwist 1260.
Winter Olympics stars.Lindsey Vonn: The American skier has 82 World Cup wins, the most for any woman, and she raced on despite a string of serious injuries.
Winter Olympics stars.Mikaela Shiffrin: The slalom specialist passed 100 World Cup wins, more than any alpine skier, and won Olympic gold at age 18.
Winter Olympics stars.Bode Miller: The American alpine skier was famed for a wild, risk-taking style and won six Olympic medals, including gold in the 2010 super-combined.
Winter Olympics stars.Chloe Kim: The snowboarder won Olympic halfpipe gold at 17 in 2018, and defended it four years later; she was also famously tweeting about ice cream mid-event.
Winter Olympics stars.Eileen Gu: The freestyle skier born in San Francisco won three medals at Beijing 2022 as a teenager, and has also modelled.
Winter Olympics stars.Apolo Ohno: The short-track speed skater won eight Olympic medals, more than any other American winter athlete at the time.
Winter Olympics stars.Eric Heiden: At the 1980 Lake Placid Olympics he won all five speed skating events, from 500 m to 10,000 m, setting four Olympic records.
Winter Olympics stars.Katarina Witt: The East German figure skater won back-to-back Olympic golds, in 1984 and 1988, and was also known for her theatrical performances.
Winter Olympics stars.Michelle Kwan: A figure skater who won five world titles and two Olympic medals but never gold, yet remains one of the sport's best-loved champions.
Winter Olympics stars.Marit Bjorgen: The Norwegian cross-country skier has won more Olympic medals than any other winter athlete, 15, and eight of them are gold.
Winter Olympics stars.Eddie the Eagle: Eddie Edwards, Britain's only ski jumper at 1988, finished last in both events, and the Games rules were changed after him.
Winter Olympics stars.Michael Phelps: He's a swimmer with 23 Olympic golds, all in summer, and the Winter Games have no pool.
Winter Olympics stars.Usain Bolt: The fastest sprinter ever, a summer star only, with his eight Olympic golds all coming on the track.
Winter Olympics stars.Simone Biles: A gymnast with a signature skill named after her, a Summer Games star who competes indoors, no snow involved.
Winter Olympics stars.Tony Hawk: The skateboarder landed the first 900 in 1999. He's famous on wheels and not snow, though his X Games rival Shaun White crosses over.
Winter Olympics stars.Kelly Slater: The surfer has won 11 world titles, and he's a legend of waves rather than winter slopes.
Winter Olympics stars.Carl Lewis: The sprinter and long jumper won nine Olympic golds, in the summer track programme.
Winter Olympics stars.Serena Williams: She won 23 Grand Slam singles titles in the Open era, a record for the era, and played Olympic tennis, a summer sport.
Winter Olympics stars.Tiger Woods: The golfer has 15 major championships, and golf, which returned to the Olympics in 2016, is not a winter sport.
Winter Olympics stars.Mo Farah: The runner won double golds in two Olympic Games, on a summer track.
Winter Olympics stars.Greg Louganis: The diver won golds in 1984 and 1988, and diving is a summer sport, in a pool.
Winter Olympics stars.Nadia Comaneci: The Romanian gymnast's perfect 10 at Montreal 1976 came in a summer Olympics, and none of her medals were won in winter.
Winter Olympics stars.Ian Thorpe: The Australian swimmer won five Olympic golds, and swimming is a summer sport, so no ice for him.

Ancient Greek philosophers.Socrates: He wrote nothing himself; we know him through Plato's dialogues. Athens sentenced him to death by hemlock for corrupting the youth.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Plato: Founded the Academy in Athens, often called the first university in the West, and it kept running for nearly 900 years.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Aristotle: Tutor to the young Alexander the Great, he also founded the Lyceum and wrote on everything from logic to marine biology.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Pythagoras: His followers formed a secretive community that reportedly refused to eat beans. The famous theorem was known in Babylon long before him.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Diogenes: He lived in a large jar and, legend says, told Alexander the Great to step aside because he was blocking the sunlight.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Epicurus: He taught that the goal of life is calm freedom from fear and pain, not luxury. Simple bread and cheese counted as a feast to him.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Heraclitus: Famed for the idea that you cannot step into the same river twice, he saw constant change as the heart of the universe.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Thales: Often called the first philosopher, he is said to have predicted a solar eclipse and measured pyramid heights using their shadows.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Zeno: His paradoxes, like Achilles never catching a tortoise, puzzled thinkers for centuries. Zeno of Citium separately founded Stoicism.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Democritus: He argued that everything is made of tiny indivisible particles called atoms, over 2,000 years before modern atomic theory.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Confucius: A trap: he was Chinese, not Greek. His sayings were gathered into the Analects, and his ideas shaped East Asian society for millennia.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Seneca: A Roman Stoic, tutor and adviser to Emperor Nero. Nero eventually ordered him to take his own life.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Cicero: Roman, not Greek: a statesman famed as the greatest orator of Rome, who helped bring Greek philosophy into Latin.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Marcus Aurelius: A Roman emperor who wrote Meditations, a private Stoic journal never meant for readers, though he wrote it in Greek.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Descartes: A French thinker of the 1600s behind "I think, therefore I am." He also gave us the x-y coordinate graph.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Kant: This German philosopher of the 1700s was so punctual that neighbors reportedly set their clocks by his daily walk.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Nietzsche: A 19th-century German who declared "God is dead." Modern, not ancient, and he was a trained scholar of classical Greek.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Lao Tzu: The legendary Chinese sage credited with the Tao Te Ching, a short book of about 5,000 characters. Not Greek.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Machiavelli: A Florentine of the 1500s whose book The Prince made his name a byword for cunning politics.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Voltaire: A French Enlightenment writer who championed free speech and religious tolerance, and whose real name was François-Marie Arouet.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Homer: He is the poet of the Iliad and Odyssey, not a philosopher. Whether one man composed both epics is still debated.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Sophocles: An Athenian playwright, not a philosopher, who wrote Oedipus the King. Only seven of his many tragedies survive complete.
Ancient Greek philosophers.John Locke: An English thinker of the 1600s who argued for natural rights to life, liberty and property, ideas that inspired the American founders.
Ancient Greek philosophers.Spinoza: A 17th-century Dutch philosopher expelled from his Jewish community in Amsterdam. He made his living grinding optical lenses.

Knights of the Round Table.Lancelot: The greatest knight of the table, whose affair with Queen Guinevere helped bring Camelot down. He is a later French addition to the legend.
Knights of the Round Table.Gawain: Arthur's nephew and hero of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, in which he must face a beheading game against a giant green challenger.
Knights of the Round Table.Galahad: Lancelot's son, pure of heart, who was the one knight worthy to complete the quest for the Holy Grail.
Knights of the Round Table.Percival: A naive young knight who finds the Grail castle but fails to ask the right question, an early version of the story by Chrétien de Troyes.
Knights of the Round Table.Tristan: Known for his doomed love of Iseult, a tale so popular it inspired Wagner's famous opera Tristan und Isolde.
Knights of the Round Table.Bedivere: He was the last knight with the dying Arthur and, in many tellings, threw Excalibur back into the lake at the king's command.
Knights of the Round Table.Kay: Arthur's foster brother and seneschal, often a sharp-tongued grump. In some tales he was the boy whose sword Arthur fetched.
Knights of the Round Table.Gareth: He arrived at court disguised as a kitchen worker and was nicknamed Beaumains, "fair hands," before proving himself a knight.
Knights of the Round Table.Bors: One of the three knights who saw the Grail, and the only one of them to return to Camelot to tell about it.
Knights of the Round Table.Merlin: Arthur's wizard and adviser, but never a knight. He was said to be the son of a mortal woman and a demon.
Knights of the Round Table.Robin Hood: An English outlaw of Sherwood Forest, tied to Nottingham, not Camelot. His stories are older than most tales of Arthur's table.
Knights of the Round Table.Ivanhoe: A knight from Walter Scott's 1819 novel set under Richard the Lionheart, long after the Arthurian age. He is fiction.
Knights of the Round Table.Don Quixote: A Spanish gentleman who goes mad reading chivalry romances and sets off as a knight. Cervantes wrote him to mock them.
Knights of the Round Table.Beowulf: An Old English hero who kills Grendel, a Scandinavian warrior and not a knight. His poem is centuries older than Arthur's tales.
Knights of the Round Table.Roland: Charlemagne's paladin who died at Roncesvalles, famed for blowing his horn too late. He belongs to a different legend cycle.
Knights of the Round Table.El Cid: A real 11th-century Castilian warlord whose title comes from Arabic for "the lord." Spain's national epic honors him.
Knights of the Round Table.Guinevere: Arthur's queen and so a fixture of Camelot, but a queen, not a knight at the table.
Knights of the Round Table.Morgan le Fay: Arthur's half-sister, a powerful sorceress and healer, who sometimes helps him and sometimes plots against him. Not a knight.
Knights of the Round Table.Little John: One of Robin Hood's band of Merry Men, famed with a quarterstaff. His nickname is ironic, as he's very tall.
Knights of the Round Table.Siegfried: A German dragon-slayer of the Nibelungenlied who bathed in dragon blood. His story belongs to Germanic legend, not Camelot.
Knights of the Round Table.Sancho Panza: The earthy squire of Don Quixote, a farmer who follows his master hoping to win an island to govern.
Knights of the Round Table.Friar Tuck: The jolly, sword-wielding monk who joins Robin Hood in Sherwood. He is an outlaw, not an Arthurian knight.
Knights of the Round Table.William Wallace: A real Scottish leader who beat the English at Stirling Bridge in 1297. He was executed in 1305, and he fought long after Arthur's era.
Knights of the Round Table.Lady of the Lake: A mystical figure who gives Arthur Excalibur, and who in some tales raises Lancelot. She is an enchantress, not a knight.

Appliances you plug into a wall.Toaster: Its glowing wires are usually nichrome, an alloy of nickel and chromium that resists electricity, and so heats up without burning out.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Kettle: Electric kettles first appeared in the 1890s, and in the UK a TV pickup surge happens at halftime when millions switch kettles on.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Hair dryer: A heating element and fan, and the first handheld hair dryers came out around 1920, long before they were common.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Desk lamp: The Anglepoise lamp, patented in 1930s Britain, used springs to hold any position and is still iconic.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Blender: Stephen Poplawski invented the blender in 1922 for making soda fountain drinks, and its spinning blades work at very high speeds.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Microwave: Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar melting near radar equipment in the 1940s, which led to the first microwave oven.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Clothes iron: Before electric irons, people heated solid irons on a stove, and the electric version was patented in 1882.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Television: Early sets were boxes with small screens, but modern ones are thin because flat displays replaced bulky glass tubes.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Refrigerator: It runs nonstop, and a fridge is likely among a home's longest-running appliances, cooling with a refrigerant that evaporates and condenses.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Space heater: A portable heater that turns almost all its electricity into heat, but costs a lot to run compared to central heating.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Slow cooker: Introduced as the Crock-Pot in the early 1970s, it simmers food for hours at low heat.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Waffle maker: A hinged heated iron that cooks batter in a grid, and waffle irons have been used since medieval times, over fires.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Candle: Trap: it makes light by burning wax, so no electricity is required.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Broom: Trap: it works through muscle power alone, and in folklore it famously carries witches.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Flashlight: Trap: runs on batteries, so it needs no wall socket. Americans call it flashlight, British call it a torch.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Abacus: Trap: this bead frame calculator needs no power, and skilled users can rival electronic calculators in speed.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Wind-up clock: Trap: powered by a spring you wind by hand, and so no plug is needed.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Whisk: Trap: this hand-held tool needs only your arm, though electric mixers are the plug-in cousin.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Rolling pin: Trap: pure muscle power, so no plug. Some bakers prefer French-style tapered pins without handles for better feel of the dough.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Paper fan: Trap: waved by hand, and some folding fans are quite old, in Japan they were used for ritual purposes.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Mop: Trap: it needs only a bucket and effort, no electricity.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Hand saw: Trap: powered by your arm, unlike its electric cousin the circular saw.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Hourglass: Trap: sand running through a narrow neck measures time with no power, and a classic hourglass runs for an hour or so.
Appliances you plug into a wall.Sundial: Trap: measures time using only sunlight and a shadow, and the oldest known examples are Egyptian.

Things usually sold in pairs.Socks: Socks are almost always sold as a pair because left and right feet are the same shape, and mismatched ones are a famous laundry mystery.
Things usually sold in pairs.Shoes: Shoes are not mirror copies; most people's feet differ slightly in size, so one shoe often fits a touch tighter than the other.
Things usually sold in pairs.Gloves: Gloves come in left and right hand versions, but early gloves were made identical and only molded to the hand with wear.
Things usually sold in pairs.Earrings: Earrings are sold as pairs, though a single stud has been a fashion choice, and some people wear just one on purpose.
Things usually sold in pairs.Chopsticks: Chopsticks are sold in pairs, and they have been used in China for over three thousand years.
Things usually sold in pairs.Mittens: Mittens warm better than gloves because fingers share heat; sold in pairs, many have a cord so you never lose one.
Things usually sold in pairs.Slippers: Slippers are sold as a pair even though many designs are identical left to right, so they work on either foot.
Things usually sold in pairs.Boots: Boots are sold in pairs, and most are cut from separate left and right lasts, wooden or plastic foot-shaped forms.
Things usually sold in pairs.Flip-flops: Flip-flops got their name from the slapping sound they make; the modern rubber version was inspired by Japanese zori sandals.
Things usually sold in pairs.Ice skates: Skate blades are not flat: a shallow groove along the bottom creates two edges that bite into the ice for turning.
Things usually sold in pairs.Roller skates: Roller skates were invented in the 1700s, and the first practical four-wheel quad version arrived in 1863.
Things usually sold in pairs.Hat: A hat is worn singly, so it is sold alone, though a cap and a scarf are often boxed as a set.
Things usually sold in pairs.Belt: You only need one belt at a time, so it is sold alone, although a few people famously wear suspenders as well.
Things usually sold in pairs.Watch: A watch goes on one wrist, so it is sold alone; people who wear two watches often do it to track two time zones.
Things usually sold in pairs.Necklace: A necklace is worn one at a time or layered, and it is sold as a single piece, unlike earrings.
Things usually sold in pairs.Scarf: A scarf is one long strip and is sold alone, even though it is as symmetrical as a pair of gloves.
Things usually sold in pairs.Necktie: A necktie is single by nature, and surprisingly its ancestor was a Croatian soldier's cravat in the 1600s.
Things usually sold in pairs.Umbrella: One umbrella is enough for the rain, although two people crammed under it will say you need a bigger one.
Things usually sold in pairs.Backpack: A backpack carries on both shoulders, but it is a single object, so it is sold alone despite two straps.
Things usually sold in pairs.Wallet: A wallet is one pocket item, sold alone; thin ones are designed so they do not warp your seating posture.
Things usually sold in pairs.Toothbrush: Toothbrushes are sold singly or in multipacks, and dentists suggest replacing yours about every three months.
Things usually sold in pairs.Apron: An apron is one piece with two ties; it is not sold as a pair even though it ties on both sides.
Things usually sold in pairs.Bow tie: A bow tie is sold singly, and the self-tie version is a famously tricky knot that many wearers skip.
Things usually sold in pairs.Headband: Headbands are sold singly or in sets, but you wear just one, so they are not a natural pair like gloves.

Cleaning tools.Mop: Mop heads of cotton strands have been used for centuries, and microfiber heads pick up more dirt with less water.
Cleaning tools.Broom: Sweeping brooms were once made of the broom plant, and a 'besom' of twigs is the witch's classic.
Cleaning tools.Sponge: Many kitchen sponges are synthetic, and a sponge can hold more bacteria than almost anything else in a kitchen.
Cleaning tools.Dustpan: A dustpan has a thin front edge to slide under dirt, and many have a rubber lip for the same reason.
Cleaning tools.Vacuum cleaner: Hubert Cecil Booth's 1901 vacuum was so large it was pulled by horses and the tubes were fed through windows.
Cleaning tools.Feather duster: Ostrich feathers are favored because they're covered with fine barbs that hold static electricity, which attracts dust.
Cleaning tools.Squeegee: A squeegee's rubber blade pushes water off a surface in one sweep, which is why window washers use it.
Cleaning tools.Scrub brush: Stiff bristles are good at loosening grime, and a scrub brush is far more efficient than a cloth on rough surfaces.
Cleaning tools.Microfiber cloth: Its fibers are about a hundredth the width of a human hair, and the tiny gaps pick up grime and oils.
Cleaning tools.Mop bucket: Many have a wringer built in, which squeezes out extra water before you mop.
Cleaning tools.Steel wool: Steel wool is fine steel strands, and it can cut through burnt-on grease, but it also scratches non-stick pans.
Cleaning tools.Lint roller: Lint rollers use sticky paper that peels off in sheets, and the idea was invented in 1956 by Nicholas McKay, an inventor.
Cleaning tools.Toilet brush: Its bristles are usually kept in a holder, and the dome shape is made to reach under the rim.
Cleaning tools.Ladle: A ladle is for serving soup, and it has nothing to do with cleaning.
Cleaning tools.Whisk: A whisk mixes eggs and batter, and the thin wire loops make it a kitchen tool, not a cleaning one.
Cleaning tools.Spatula: A spatula flips pancakes, and although it can scrape a bowl clean, it's a cooking tool.
Cleaning tools.Rolling pin: A rolling pin flattens dough, and has been used for centuries in baking.
Cleaning tools.Grater: A grater shreds cheese and vegetables, and it can be a pain to clean afterward.
Cleaning tools.Tongs: Tongs grip hot food or ice, and they work as extensions of the fingers.
Cleaning tools.Colander: A colander drains pasta and washes vegetables, so it's a food tool and not a cleaning tool.
Cleaning tools.Peeler: The Y-shaped peeler removes just the skin of a fruit, and it saves much more flesh than a knife.
Cleaning tools.Corkscrew: The corkscrew was inspired by the musket-cleaning screw in the 1600s, and was patented in 1795.
Cleaning tools.Garlic press: A garlic press crushes cloves, but many cooks find it more trouble to clean than to use.
Cleaning tools.Funnel: A funnel guides liquid into small openings, and it's a kitchen and garage tool rather than a cleaning one.

Things with numbers printed on them.Clock: The 12-hour face traces back to ancient Egyptian and Babylonian counting, and 12 divides neatly by 2, 3, 4 and 6.
Things with numbers printed on them.Calculator: Pocket calculators arrived in the early 1970s, and the early ones cost hundreds of dollars, close to a month's pay for many.
Things with numbers printed on them.Ruler: Metric rulers are marked in millimeters, and the meter itself was once defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from pole to equator.
Things with numbers printed on them.Thermometer: Fahrenheit's thermometers used mercury, and his scale was set with 0 at a brine freezing mix and 96 near body temperature.
Things with numbers printed on them.Calendar: Our calendar skipped 11 days in 1752 when Britain adopted the Gregorian system, so September 2 was followed by September 14.
Things with numbers printed on them.TV remote: The average remote has around 40 buttons, and the number keys are there for the channels you can dial directly.
Things with numbers printed on them.Lottery ticket: Your odds of winning a big jackpot may be hundreds of millions to one, so you are likelier to be struck by lightning.
Things with numbers printed on them.Coin: Coins have numbers for value and year, and the ridges on a coin's edge were first added to stop people shaving off precious metal.
Things with numbers printed on them.Banknote: Each banknote carries a unique serial number, and modern notes hide numbers and security threads to stop forgers.
Things with numbers printed on them.Tape measure: The first measuring tapes were cloth or leather, and the metal retractable kind arrived in the 19th century.
Things with numbers printed on them.Measuring jug: Many jugs show cups, milliliters and ounces, and a US cup is about 240 milliliters, not the same as other nations.
Things with numbers printed on them.Bathroom scale: Modern scales use strain gauges, small sensors whose electrical resistance changes slightly as you stand on them.
Things with numbers printed on them.Phone keypad: The 3-by-4 telephone pad was chosen in the 1960s after tests, and calculators put 7-8-9 at the top, making them opposites.
Things with numbers printed on them.Fork: A plain fork carries no numbers; the forks in a place setting are ordered outside-in by course, but nothing is printed on them.
Things with numbers printed on them.Pillow: Pillows hold stuffing, not numbers, though a plain pillow's tag carries a fill rating that most people never look at.
Things with numbers printed on them.Sponge: Sea sponges are animals with no brain, and real ones have been used for washing for thousands of years.
Things with numbers printed on them.Broom: Witches' flying brooms are folklore, and a real broom is made of plain bristles rather than markings.
Things with numbers printed on them.Towel: Douglas Adams made a towel the most useful item for an interstellar hitchhiker, but the real one carries no numbers.
Things with numbers printed on them.Spoon: Spoons predate forks by thousands of years, and the oldest examples are carved from wood, bone and shell.
Things with numbers printed on them.Sock: A sock may have a size on its band, but the sock itself isn't printed with numbers, and many go missing in the wash.
Things with numbers printed on them.Comb: The comb is among the oldest personal items, and its teeth bear no digits, unlike a ruler.
Things with numbers printed on them.Toothbrush: Bristles were once boar hair, and nylon replaced them in 1938, but nothing is numbered on the handle.
Things with numbers printed on them.Napkin: Napkins carry no numbers, and the word comes from an old French word for a small tablecloth.
Things with numbers printed on them.Plunger: A plunger is a rubber cup on a stick, and there is no printed digit on it, though the flange type is made for toilets.

Other words for a toilet.Loo: 'Loo' is a British favorite, and its origin is debated; one theory credits the French 'gardez l'eau' and another the word 'lieu', place.
Other words for a toilet.Restroom: 'Restroom' is American politeness at work, though nobody actually goes there to rest.
Other words for a toilet.Lavatory: 'Lavatory' comes from the Latin 'lavare', to wash, and is the usual word on aircraft signs.
Other words for a toilet.WC: 'WC' stands for water closet, a term from the 1800s that remains common on signs across Europe.
Other words for a toilet.Washroom: 'Washroom' is the standard word in Canada, where it covers any public bathroom.
Other words for a toilet.Latrine: A latrine is a simple pit or trench toilet, long used by armies and camps.
Other words for a toilet.Privy: A privy is an old word for an outdoor toilet, derived from 'private'.
Other words for a toilet.Commode: A commode can mean a chest of drawers or a toilet, and it was long a piece of furniture with a chamber pot inside.
Other words for a toilet.Powder room: A powder room is a small guest toilet, named for a place where women once powdered their noses.
Other words for a toilet.Outhouse: An outhouse is a small toilet shed built outside the main house, and many still exist in rural areas.
Other words for a toilet.Water closet: The water closet was a big upgrade: Sir John Harington built a flushing toilet for Queen Elizabeth I around 1596.
Other words for a toilet.Ladies' room: 'Ladies' room' is a polite American euphemism, one of many words people have invented to avoid saying toilet.
Other words for a toilet.Pantry: A pantry stores food, and the word comes from Latin for bread, so it is far from the bathroom.
Other words for a toilet.Scullery: A scullery was where dishes and pots got scrubbed in old British houses, so water, but not toilets.
Other words for a toilet.Larder: A larder is a cool room for storing meat and dairy, which kept food safe before refrigerators.
Other words for a toilet.Parlor: A parlor was the best room for receiving guests, so it was the one place you'd hide the chamber pot.
Other words for a toilet.Foyer: A foyer is the entrance hall, and the word comes from French for 'hearth' or 'home'.
Other words for a toilet.Attic: An attic sits under the roof; the term comes from Attica, Greece, thanks to a style of architecture.
Other words for a toilet.Cellar: A cellar is an underground storeroom, often used for wine, and its Latin root means a storehouse.
Other words for a toilet.Den: A den is a cozy private room for relaxing, borrowed from the word for an animal's lair.
Other words for a toilet.Vestibule: A vestibule is an entry space between outside and inside, helping keep drafts out of buildings.
Other words for a toilet.Nook: A nook is a small corner, usually for sitting, and it's not a room built for plumbing.
Other words for a toilet.Alcove: An alcove is a recess in a wall, and the word comes from the Arabic 'al-qubba', meaning vault.
Other words for a toilet.Loft: A loft is an upper room under the roof, or in cities a converted industrial space.

Houseplants.Spider plant: Spider plants send out baby plantlets on long stems, and NASA tested them for cleaning indoor air.
Houseplants.Snake plant: Snake plants survive weeks of neglect and release oxygen at night, unusual among plants.
Houseplants.Peace lily: Peace lilies droop dramatically when thirsty and perk up within hours of watering.
Houseplants.Pothos: Pothos is so tough it's sometimes called devil's ivy, as it stays green even in dim rooms.
Houseplants.Monstera: Monstera's leaf holes may help it withstand strong winds and let light reach lower leaves.
Houseplants.Rubber plant: Rubber plants are a relative of fig trees, and their milky sap is the origin of the name.
Houseplants.Fiddle-leaf fig: Fiddle-leaf figs are famously fussy, and they hate being moved or overwatered.
Houseplants.Aloe vera: Aloe vera's gel has been used on burns for centuries, and it stores water in thick leaves.
Houseplants.Jade plant: Jade plants can live for decades, and some are passed down through families.
Houseplants.ZZ plant: ZZ plants store water in their thick underground rhizomes, so they survive long droughts.
Houseplants.Boston fern: Boston ferns like humidity, and were a popular Victorian parlor plant.
Houseplants.Moth orchid: Moth orchids can rebloom for years if you keep them in bright, indirect light.
Houseplants.Oak: An oak can live for hundreds of years and is far too big to keep indoors.
Houseplants.Corn: Corn is a giant grass that needs open fields and summer sun, not a windowsill.
Houseplants.Pumpkin: A pumpkin vine can sprawl across a garden, and the fruit is technically a berry.
Houseplants.Apple tree: An apple tree needs winter cold to fruit, which is why it fails indoors.
Houseplants.Wheat: Wheat is a field grass, and entire fields are needed to feed bread makers.
Houseplants.Redwood: Coast redwoods can top 100 meters, so no living room will hold one.
Houseplants.Potato: Potatoes are tubers that grow underground, not a decorative plant.
Houseplants.Seaweed: Seaweed is a marine alga that needs salt water and doesn't grow in pots.
Houseplants.Maple: Maple trees grow tall outdoors and are far from a pot on a shelf.
Houseplants.Cabbage: Cabbage is a vegetable and a garden crop, not a houseplant.
Houseplants.Sunflower: Sunflowers follow the sun when young, but they grow too tall to keep indoors.
Houseplants.Weeping willow: Weeping willows need a lot of water and space, so they stay in parks and by rivers.

Things stuck on a fridge door.Fridge magnets: Fridge magnets became a popular souvenir in the 1970s, and the door is a giant display for them.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Kid's drawing: A child's drawing on the fridge is a tradition in many homes, and it signals to kids that their work matters.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Takeout menu: A takeout menu clings on by a magnet, so the number's handy when nobody feels like cooking.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Calendar: A calendar on the fridge keeps the household's plans in one place everyone passes each day.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Family photo: A family photo on the fridge is a favorite spot for pictures, since everyone sees it daily.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Shopping list: A shopping list gets stuck on the fridge because that's where you see what's missing.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Postcard: Postcards are often pinned up as souvenirs, and the fridge door has become a gallery.
Things stuck on a fridge door.School schedule: A school schedule is on the fridge so parents can keep track of the week.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Wedding invite: A wedding invite stays on the fridge until the day, as a reminder to RSVP.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Appointment card: An appointment card is posted on the fridge so it doesn't get forgotten.
Things stuck on a fridge door.To-do list: A to-do list on the fridge door is hard to miss, and that's the point.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Report card: A report card on the fridge is a proud parent's moment.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Rug: A rug belongs on the floor, and magnets can't hold up heavy fabric; the word comes from a Scandinavian term for coarse cloth.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Houseplant: A houseplant needs soil, water and light, none of which a fridge door offers, though a fridge top can be warm and dry.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Wallpaper: Wallpaper is glued across whole walls and was once hand-painted in China long before it reached Europe.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Light switch: A light switch is wired into the wall's electrical box and can't be moved, so it never ends up on the fridge door.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Oil painting: An oil painting is far too heavy for a magnet, and real ones are hung from wires on the wall with strong hooks.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Curtains: Curtains hang from a rod to block light, and some historic ones were once used to keep out draughts as well.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Doorbell: A doorbell is wired into the house and was invented in the 1800s, but it sits by the front door and not on a fridge.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Thermostat: A thermostat is wired to the heating system, and it senses the room's temperature before switching the heat on or off.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Smoke alarm: A smoke alarm is fixed to the ceiling, since smoke rises, and it needs a regular battery check to stay useful.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Ceiling fan: A ceiling fan is bolted to a joist, and it can make a room feel several degrees cooler without changing its temperature.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Coat hook: A coat hook is screwed into a wall or door, and the sturdy kind can hold many kilograms, much more than a fridge magnet.
Things stuck on a fridge door.Window blinds: Window blinds are fitted into a window frame to control light, and the fridge door has nothing like a window.

Body parts humans DON'T have.Tusks: Tusks are elongated teeth, as in elephants and walruses, and humans have none.

Body parts humans DON'T have.Tailbone: Humans do have a tailbone, the coccyx, a few fused vertebrae left from our ancestors' tails.
Body parts humans DON'T have.Appendix: We do have an appendix, which sits at the start of the large intestine.

Non-animals that have a neck.Bottle: A bottle's neck is the narrow top part, and its shape helps pouring and keeps a stopper tight.
Non-animals that have a neck.Violin: A violin's neck holds the fingerboard, and the scroll at the top is carved by hand; the instrument has existed since the 1500s.
Non-animals that have a neck.Cello: A cello's neck rises to a scroll, and the player holds the instrument between the knees, supported by an endpin on the floor.
Non-animals that have a neck.Banjo: A banjo's long neck attaches to a round body topped with a drumlike skin, and its roots go back to instruments brought from West Africa.
Non-animals that have a neck.Vase: A vase has a narrow neck that opens to a lip, and in pottery terms the neck is what the shoulders taper to.
Non-animals that have a neck.Ukulele: A ukulele's short neck belongs to a small four-stringed instrument that arrived in Hawaii in the 1800s with Portuguese immigrants.
Non-animals that have a neck.Bass guitar: A bass guitar's neck is longer than a regular guitar's, with thicker strings that sound an octave lower.
Non-animals that have a neck.Mandolin: A mandolin's neck bears a fretted board and eight strings tuned in pairs like a violin's four strings.
Non-animals that have a neck.Harp: A harp has a neck, the curved top piece that holds the tuning pins and anchors the strings in tension.
Non-animals that have a neck.Drum: A drum is a hollow shell with a skin stretched across it, and nothing about it narrows into a neck.
Non-animals that have a neck.Piano: A piano's strings run over a big iron frame, and its body has a lid, keys, and legs, but no neck.
Non-animals that have a neck.Plate: A plate is a flat dish whose edge slopes up into a rim, but it has no neck that narrows and rises.
Non-animals that have a neck.Tambourine: A tambourine is a circular frame with jingles and a skin; you hold the frame, which has no neck at all.
Non-animals that have a neck.Xylophone: A xylophone has bars arranged on a frame, and you strike them with mallets, with no narrow neck.
Non-animals that have a neck.Harmonica: A harmonica is a small box with reed chambers and no neck, which is why it can fit in a pocket.
Non-animals that have a neck.Bowl: A bowl is wide and open, with a body that curves into a rim, but with no narrow neck like a bottle.
Non-animals that have a neck.Brick: A solid rectangular brick has no neck, which is why a bottle's narrowed top is called a neck, a name that came from the human body.
Non-animals that have a neck.Pillow: A pillow supports your neck instead of having one, and some pillows are shaped to cradle the neck in particular.
Non-animals that have a neck.Book: A book has a spine, a cover, and pages, but no neck, even if the body-part words spine and leaf do come from it.
Non-animals that have a neck.Triangle: A triangle is a bent steel rod struck with a beater, so it is a three-sided shape with no neck.
Non-animals that have a neck.Cymbal: A cymbal is a thin brass disk with a raised dome called a bell, but nothing that could be called a neck.
Non-animals that have a neck.Maracas: Maracas are hollow gourds or shells filled with seeds on a handle, and the handle isn't called a neck.
Non-animals that have a neck.Frisbee: A Frisbee is a flat plastic disc, and its design is as simple as a plate, with no neck at all.

Things that should never be in a pool.Piranha: Piranhas are freshwater fish from South America with razor-sharp teeth, though attacks on people are rare.
Things that should never be in a pool.Shark: Most sharks live in the ocean, though bull sharks can swim up rivers and even tolerate fresh water.
Things that should never be in a pool.Hair dryer: Plugged-in electronics near water are dangerous, and modern hair dryers have a safety plug that cuts power if they fall in water.
Things that should never be in a pool.Laptop: A laptop dropped into a pool would be ruined and could short out, and its charger plugged in nearby adds a shock risk.
Things that should never be in a pool.Alligator: Alligators are freshwater predators of the southeastern United States, and now and then one turns up in a backyard Florida pool.
Things that should never be in a pool.Jellyfish: Jellyfish have stinging cells called nematocysts that can hurt even if the animal is dead.
Things that should never be in a pool.Glass bottle: Broken glass is hard to see underwater and can cut feet badly, which is why most pools ban glass at the poolside.
Things that should never be in a pool.Cactus: A cactus is covered in sharp spines that could puncture swimmers, and desert plants also hate being soaked.
Things that should never be in a pool.Sofa: A sofa soaks up water, becomes enormously heavy, and can clog a pool's filters and pumps, which is why it never belongs there.
Things that should never be in a pool.Car: A car in a pool would leak oil and fuel and weighs over a ton, so it is the ultimate pool no-no.
Things that should never be in a pool.Lawnmower: A lawnmower has sharp blades and a fuel tank that would leak into the water, so it is one more thing to keep out.
Things that should never be in a pool.Pool noodle: A pool noodle is a foam tube that floats and is made for pools, and it was invented in the 1980s.
Things that should never be in a pool.Beach ball: A beach ball is inflatable and made to float, which is why it is a perfect pool toy and is quite safe in the water.
Things that should never be in a pool.Swimmer: A swimmer is exactly who a pool is for, and swimming is one of the best whole-body exercises.
Things that should never be in a pool.Goggles: Goggles keep chlorine from stinging the eyes, and swimmers wear them to see clearly underwater.
Things that should never be in a pool.Water wings: Water wings are inflatable armbands that help kids float, though lifeguards stress that they are not a real safety device.
Things that should never be in a pool.Diving ring: A diving ring sinks to the bottom for kids to retrieve in swimming games and is built for pool use.
Things that should never be in a pool.Inflatable flamingo: Giant inflatable flamingos became a pool craze in the 2010s and are made of tough vinyl that holds up in the sun and chlorine.
Things that should never be in a pool.Kickboard: A kickboard is a foam board that swimmers hold to train their legs while keeping the arms still, a pool staple.
Things that should never be in a pool.Chlorine: Chlorine kills germs in pools, and the strong smell most people notice is actually chloramines, formed when chlorine reacts with sweat.
Things that should never be in a pool.Swim cap: A swim cap keeps hair out of the face and cuts drag, and it is required in many public pools.
Things that should never be in a pool.Lane rope: Lane ropes have rotating discs that calm waves and keep a race fair, helping swimmers go faster.
Things that should never be in a pool.Pool float: A pool float lets swimmers lounge on the water, and the first inflatable pool toys appeared in the 20th century.

Things that are slippery.Banana peel: The banana peel gag is real: its inner layer has a slippery gel, and studies measured it among the slickest natural surfaces.
Things that are slippery.Ice: Ice is slippery thanks to a thin film of water on its surface, and that film exists even well below freezing.
Things that are slippery.Soap: Soap is slippery since it forms a thin lubricating film with water, which is also what lifts dirt from your skin.
Things that are slippery.Wet floor: A wet floor is slippery since water fills the tiny gaps between your shoe and the surface, cutting friction and grip.
Things that are slippery.Eel: An eel is slippery because of mucus, and it can wriggle out of a grip, sometimes even leaving the water to cross land.
Things that are slippery.Oil spill: Oil floats and spreads into a thin slick on water; even a small spill can cover a surprisingly large area of sea.
Things that are slippery.Butter: Butter is slippery because its fat is soft at room temperature, and it melts at around body temperature.
Things that are slippery.Frozen pond: A frozen pond is slippery, and it is only safe to walk on once the ice is thick; about 10 centimeters is a common guideline.
Things that are slippery.Waterslide: A waterslide keeps friction low by running a thin sheet of water over smooth plastic, so riders can reach real speed.
Things that are slippery.Wet rock: Wet rock near a river or sea is slippery because of a thin algae film, one of the main causes of hiking falls.
Things that are slippery.Ice rink: Ice rinks are kept just below freezing, and a skater's blade glides on a thin film of meltwater.
Things that are slippery.Sandpaper: Sandpaper has an abrasive grit surface with very high friction, which is why it is used to rough surfaces up.
Things that are slippery.Velcro: Velcro was inspired by burrs stuck to a Swiss engineer's dog; tiny hooks catch loops to give it grip, not slip.
Things that are slippery.Rubber mat: Rubber has high friction against most surfaces, so mats are laid where grip matters, like under bathtubs.
Things that are slippery.Carpet: Carpet's fibers grip shoe soles and add friction, and it traps dust and allergens far better than a hard floor does.
Things that are slippery.Grip tape: Grip tape is sandpaper-like coating on a skateboard deck, and it exists to keep your feet firmly in place.
Things that are slippery.Brick: Brick has a rough surface, so it gives good grip when dry, though it can still turn slippery under moss or algae.
Things that are slippery.Sneaker sole: Sneaker soles use rubber with a tread pattern that channels water out, to grip surfaces rather than slide.
Things that are slippery.Climbing chalk: Climbers use chalk, magnesium carbonate, to dry sweat from their hands and give more grip on holds.
Things that are slippery.Doormat: A doormat has a rough, bristly surface made to scrape mud off shoes and give your feet good traction.
Things that are slippery.Tree bark: Tree bark is rough and ridged, and each species has its own pattern, so bark helps identify trees in winter.
Things that are slippery.Yoga mat: A yoga mat has a textured, sticky surface so hands and feet will not slide in downward dog.
Things that are slippery.Cork board: Cork is naturally grippy, and the same springy cells that let pins stay in a board give it a non-slip surface.
Things that are slippery.Emery board: An emery board is coated with emery, a gritty natural abrasive, so it is rough on purpose to file nails.

Surnames that are also job titles.Cook: Captain James Cook mapped much of the Pacific. Cook is among the most widespread job surnames in English-speaking countries.
Surnames that are also job titles.Carpenter: Carpenter is among the common job surnames. It comes from the old French word for a wood worker, and Karen Carpenter made it famous in song.
Surnames that are also job titles.Mason: A stoneworker's name, which became a given name in recent decades. It's now among the most popular boys' names in the US.
Surnames that are also job titles.Miller: Miller is one of the most frequent English surnames. Mills were central to every medieval village, so millers were everywhere.
Surnames that are also job titles.Butcher: A meat seller, and a common surname. The word derives from Old French for a goat slaughterer.
Surnames that are also job titles.Porter: A carrier of loads or a doorkeeper, giving the name. Porter is also a dark beer once favored by London's street and river porters.
Surnames that are also job titles.Turner: A craftsman who worked a lathe. The painter J.M.W. Turner carries it, though his own father was a barber.
Surnames that are also job titles.Archer: A bowman. Archers were vital in medieval English armies, as longbows won battles such as Agincourt in 1415.
Surnames that are also job titles.Hunter: One who hunts. A surname for those who supplied game, and today a popular first name too.
Surnames that are also job titles.Potter: A maker of pots, hence the surname. Harry Potter's author said she chose it from a childhood neighbor family.
Surnames that are also job titles.Shepherd: The sheep herder. A shepherd's staff curved at the top is called a crook, which gave us the word 'crook' for a bent person.
Surnames that are also job titles.Fisher: One who fishes. Often paired with Fisherman in naming, it's still a widely used surname.
Surnames that are also job titles.Weaver: A cloth maker. The surname spread widely because weaving was a main medieval trade across Europe.
Surnames that are also job titles.Johnson: Means 'son of John', a patronymic rather than a trade. It's among the top surnames in the US.
Surnames that are also job titles.Williams: From 'son of William'. It's a patronymic name, not a job, and very common in Wales and England.
Surnames that are also job titles.Brown: From a hair or skin color, not an occupation. It's among the most common surnames in the English-speaking world.
Surnames that are also job titles.Davis: A patronymic meaning 'son of David'. Davis is especially common in the US and Wales.
Surnames that are also job titles.Wilson: Means 'son of Will'. It names a father's first name, not a trade.
Surnames that are also job titles.Garcia: A Spanish surname of uncertain origin, possibly Basque. It's one of the most common in the Spanish-speaking world.
Surnames that are also job titles.Martinez: Spanish for 'son of Martin'. It's a patronymic, not a profession.
Surnames that are also job titles.Anderson: Means 'son of Andrew', and is widespread in Scandinavia and Scotland. It's a family-line name, not a trade.
Surnames that are also job titles.Thompson: Means 'son of Thomas'. Another patronymic, it's one of the most common English surnames.
Surnames that are also job titles.Jackson: Means 'son of Jack'. It's a family name, not an occupation, and named a US president.

Things in an airplane cockpit.Yoke: The control wheel pilots pull and push. Its name comes from the old farm harness, since early planes were controlled with such bars.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Throttle: The lever that sets engine power. Pilots push it forward for takeoff, and it often has several for multi-engine aircraft.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Altimeter: Measures altitude using air pressure. Pilots must adjust it for local weather, as pressure changes can throw it off.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Rudder pedals: Foot pedals that swing the tail rudder left or right. They also work the nosewheel on the ground.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Autopilot: It holds a heading and altitude, and some can even land the plane. Pilots still monitor it closely throughout.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Headset: Pilots use noise-cancelling headsets to hear radio calls over engine noise. The microphone sits right by the mouth.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Compass: A magnetic compass is a backup instrument. It dips and swings in turns, so pilots rely on gyro-based heading indicators.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Artificial horizon: Also called an attitude indicator, it shows the plane's tilt relative to the ground. It's vital when clouds hide the real horizon.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Fuel gauge: Shows how much fuel is in the tanks. Pilots cross-check it with flight-time calculations rather than trusting it blindly.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Airspeed indicator: Reads speed using air pressure from a forward-facing tube. Blocked tubes have caused serious accidents.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Flight computer: A modern cockpit computer manages routes and fuel. Older ones were circular slide rules pilots used for navigation.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Galley: The cabin's kitchen. A galley has trolleys and ovens for passenger meals, and it's behind the cockpit door.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Overhead bin: Storage above passenger seats. It's in the cabin, not up front.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Tray table: The fold-down table at your seat. Not in the cockpit.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Lavatory: The restroom is for passengers. Airplane toilets use a vacuum system to flush with little water.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Drinks trolley: The cart that cabin crew roll down the aisle. It's a cabin item and no pilot gear.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Baggage carousel: The belt loop in the terminal where bags appear. It's an airport item, not an aircraft one.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Jet bridge: The covered walkway connecting a terminal and plane door. It's attached to the airport, not found in the cockpit.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Check-in desk: Where passengers drop bags and get boarding passes. It's in the terminal.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Conveyor belt: Moves luggage through airports. It sits at ground level, never in an aircraft cockpit.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Departure board: Lists flights in the terminal. Pilots rely on dispatch and radios, not this board.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Duty-free shop: Sells tax-free goods in the terminal. Not on the flight deck.
Things in an airplane cockpit.In-flight magazine: Found in seat pockets, ads and all. Passengers read it, not pilots.
Things in an airplane cockpit.Passport control: Immigration checks at airports. It happens on the ground, never in the cockpit.

Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Helmet: Knights' helmets changed over time, from simple nasal helms to the elaborate great helm and later bascinet.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Shield: Shields carried a knight's heraldic design, which is how people recognized him when his face was hidden by a helmet.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Sword: Knights' swords were not as heavy as people think, and a typical one weighed only about one to two kilograms.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Lance: A lance was a long spear used in a charge on horseback and also for jousting at tournaments.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Chain mail: Mail was made of thousands of interlinked iron rings, and a full shirt could take months to make by hand.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Gauntlets: Gauntlets are armored gloves, and to "throw down the gauntlet" came from tossing one to challenge someone to a duel.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Breastplate: Plate armor looked heavy, but a full suit was usually 20 to 25 kilograms, spread across the body.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Spurs: Spurs were a knight's trademark, so much that "winning one's spurs" came to mean earning your knighthood.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Tabard: A tabard was a surcoat worn over the armor showing his coat of arms, and today heralds still wear them.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Visor: A visor could be lifted to reveal the face, and it lets the knight see and breathe while also protecting him in battle.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Bayonet: A bayonet fits on a gun, and as guns came into use only late, so they belong to later centuries.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Musket: Muskets arrived at the end of the Middle Ages, and they eventually made armor obsolete.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Bowler hat: The bowler hat was designed in 1849, many centuries after the Middle Ages, so a knight would never wear it.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Kevlar vest: Kevlar was invented in the 1960s, long after knights used steel plate for protection.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Night-vision goggles: Night vision is a 20th-century invention, so a knight would have had to make do with torches.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Lasso: The lasso is associated with cowboys and not knights, who preferred the lance for catching enemies.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Toga: A toga is Roman dress, from an earlier era than the Middle Ages and worn without armor.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Trident: The trident is the sea god's weapon in Roman myth and was used by gladiators, not by knights.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Boomerang: The boomerang is an Aboriginal Australian hunting tool, unknown in medieval Europe.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Top hat: Top hats were fashionable in the late 1700s and 1800s, long after medieval knights.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Monocle: The monocle came in the 1800s, so a knight would not have worn one.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Wristwatch: Wristwatches did not become common until the early 1900s, and a knight told time by the sun and church bells.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Revolver: A revolver was patented in the 1830s, centuries after the knight's golden age.
Things a medieval knight wore or carried.Sneakers: Sneakers appeared in the late 1800s, and a knight would have worn leather boots or armored shoes called sabatons.

Names of baby farm animals.Calf: A calf is a young cow, and a newborn can often stand and walk within an hour of birth.
Names of baby farm animals.Piglet: A piglet is a baby pig, and sows can have litters of a dozen or more in one go.
Names of baby farm animals.Lamb: A lamb is a young sheep, and it can recognise its mother by her bleat within a day or two.
Names of baby farm animals.Kid: A kid is a baby goat, which is also why kid became slang for a child.
Names of baby farm animals.Foal: A foal is a young horse, and it can usually stand within an hour of birth to evade predators.
Names of baby farm animals.Chick: A chick is a baby chicken, and it starts to communicate with its mother while still inside the egg.
Names of baby farm animals.Duckling: A duckling is a baby duck, and it imprints on the first moving thing it sees, usually its mother.
Names of baby farm animals.Gosling: A gosling is a baby goose, and goslings follow their parents in a line, sometimes even into a human crowd.
Names of baby farm animals.Colt: A colt is a young male horse, usually under four, and the female equivalent is a filly.
Names of baby farm animals.Filly: A filly is a young female horse, and the word goes back to an old Norse word for foal.
Names of baby farm animals.Cub: A cub is a young bear, lion, fox or wolf, but not a farm animal, so it's out of place here.
Names of baby farm animals.Joey: A joey is a baby kangaroo, and it's born so small, about the size of a jelly bean, that it crawls into its mother's pouch.
Names of baby farm animals.Toddler: A toddler is a young child, so it's not an animal, and it also goes with the human word infant.
Names of baby farm animals.Cygnet: A cygnet is a baby swan, so a wild bird, not a farm animal, with grey downy fluff.
Names of baby farm animals.Owlet: An owlet is a baby owl, so it's a wild bird and not found on a farm.
Names of baby farm animals.Eaglet: An eaglet is a baby eagle, and it's wild, so it doesn't belong in a barnyard.
Names of baby farm animals.Leveret: A leveret is a young hare, and unlike rabbits, hares are born furry with open eyes.
Names of baby farm animals.Tadpole: A tadpole is a baby frog, and it breathes through gills until it grows lungs.
Names of baby farm animals.Caterpillar: A caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly or moth, and can eat many times its own weight in leaves.
Names of baby farm animals.Nymph: A nymph is a young insect that looks like a small adult, like a grasshopper or dragonfly, so it isn't farm stock.
Names of baby farm animals.Larva: A larva is an early stage of an insect with complete metamorphosis, so it's not a farm baby.
Names of baby farm animals.Infant: An infant is a baby human, and so it isn't a farm animal.
Names of baby farm animals.Pupa: A pupa is the resting stage between larva and adult in butterflies and beetles, nothing to do with farms.
Names of baby farm animals.Spiderling: A spiderling is a baby spider, and some spiderlings travel by ballooning, floating away on silk threads.
