Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Goalkeeper: It is the only soccer position allowed to handle the ball, and keepers wear a different colored shirt to stand out.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Bookkeeper: They record a company's financial transactions, and the term goes back to when ledgers were literally big books.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Beekeeper: A hive's queen can lay up to 2,000 eggs a day, and beekeepers often wear white because bees dislike dark colors.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Shopkeeper: The phrase "nation of shopkeepers" was used to describe England, whether as an insult or as praise.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Gamekeeper: Gamekeepers look after wildlife on estates, and in the UK gamekeepers have long managed shooting estates.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Housekeeper: The job once meant running a whole large household, and the head housekeeper of a grand house oversaw all the maids.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Innkeeper: Innkeepers have a long history, and the Bible's innkeeper in the nativity story is among the best known.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Lighthouse keeper: They once tended the lamp through the night, and many lighthouses are now automatic with no keeper at all.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Timekeeper: In sports, the timekeeper runs the clock, and in the Olympics timing is taken to the thousandth of a second.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Groundskeeper: They care for sports fields, parks and estates, and top stadium pitches may need mowing patterns planned in advance.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Peacekeeper: UN peacekeepers wear blue helmets and have served in missions since 1948.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Keepsake: A keepsake is a small object kept in memory of someone, which is a thing, not a job.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Upkeep: It means the cost of maintaining something, so it is the money, not a person.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Safekeeping: It is the state of being held safely, not a person with that job.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Housekeeping: This is the work of the housekeeper, and tech uses it too, for routine system maintenance.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Bookkeeping: The activity, not the person: this is the recording of accounts, one for the bookkeeper to do.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Keep-fit: A British term for exercise classes, which are an activity, not a job.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Keepy-uppy: A children's game of keeping a ball in the air with your feet, which is a skill and not a job.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Beekeeping: The activity of tending hives, not the person; the person is the beekeeper.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Timekeeping: Being punctual or recording time is an activity, while a timekeeper is the person.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Gatekeeping: Today it means controlling access, which is behavior, not an actual occupation, even though gates once did have keepers.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Finders keepers: A saying that whoever finds something may keep it, which is a rule of thumb and not a job.
Jobs ending in 'keeper'.Keeping: It is just the activity or state of holding, and keeping is not a person or a job.

Famous robots from movies and TV.R2-D2: Sound designer Ben Burtt built R2-D2's beeps from his own voice, whistles and a synthesizer. Fans say the name came from a film reel label, Reel 2, Dialog 2.
Famous robots from movies and TV.C-3PO: C-3PO claims fluency in over six million forms of communication. Actor Anthony Daniels wore the stiff gold suit, and could barely see or sit in it.
Famous robots from movies and TV.WALL-E: The name stands for Waste Allocation Load Lifter, Earth-class. Pixar gave this almost wordless robot a soul by borrowing from silent-film comedians like Buster Keaton.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Bender: Futurama's bending robot is Bender Bending Rodriguez, built to bend girders but happiest stealing and drinking. His serial number is 1729, a famous math number.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Robby the Robot: Robby debuted in Forbidden Planet (1956) and was one of the first movie robots with real personality. He later appeared in Lost in Space and The Twilight Zone.
Famous robots from movies and TV.BB-8: This rolling droid from The Force Awakens was a real, working prop, not just CGI. Its head clung to the ball with magnets, and the effect was done on set.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Baymax: Baymax, from Big Hero 6, was inspired by soft inflatable robot arms developed at Carnegie Mellon for safe patient care. Pixar-style charm, real robotics idea.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Johnny 5: Short Circuit's Johnny 5 came alive after a lightning strike and kept demanding "Input!" The 1986 robot was a real, full-size machine built for the film, not CGI.
Famous robots from movies and TV.K-9: Doctor Who's robot dog K-9 first appeared in 1977. The prop was so hard to steer on location that its tin body famously struggled over any rough ground.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Ultron: Ultron is the Marvel villain AI created by Hank Pym in the comics. In the films, Tony Stark and Bruce Banner build him, and he decides humanity must go.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Rosie: Rosie the Robot Maid in The Jetsons did chores in a 1962 vision of 2062. Her cartoon future got stoves and vacuums right long before real robot vacuums arrived.
Famous robots from movies and TV.EVE: EVE, WALL-E's love interest, is an Extraterrestrial Vegetation Evaluator. Designers modeled her sleek look on Apple products, with white and glossy smoothness.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Sonny: In I, Robot (2004) Sonny is a unique robot who dreams and feels. Alan Tudyk performed him on set via motion capture, so the voice and movements share one actor.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Yoda: Yoda is a living being, not a machine. He is a 900-year-old Jedi Master, and in the original films he was a puppet operated and voiced by Frank Oz.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Chewbacca: Chewbacca is a Wookiee, a hairy alien, not a droid. His growls were mixed from recordings of bears, walruses and other animals by sound designer Ben Burtt.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Gollum: Gollum is a corrupted creature from Middle-earth, not a robot. Andy Serkis performed him through motion capture, a landmark in digital character acting.
E.T. is a biological alien, not a robot. His puppet had real animatronics, and his voice was built from sounds including an elderly woman's raspy breathing.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Shrek: Shrek is a flesh-and-blood ogre, not a machine. The original voice was meant to be Chris Farley, but after his death Mike Myers re-recorded it with a Scottish accent.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Groot: Groot is a tree-like alien, not a robot. Vin Diesel voices him, and despite saying only "I am Groot," he recorded each line many different ways.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Stitch: Stitch is an alien experiment, not a robot. Lilo and Stitch's creator Chris Sanders voices him himself, and the scrappy Experiment 626 became a Disney favorite.
Famous robots from movies and TV.ALF: ALF is an alien from the planet Melmac, not a robot. The TV puppet needed a performer under the set, so the show's tables were built with holes in them.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Spock: Spock is half Vulcan and half human, not a robot, despite his cool logic. Leonard Nimoy invented the Vulcan nerve pinch himself during the original series.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Gizmo: Gizmo is a furry Mogwai from Gremlins, not a robot. The film's rule "never feed them after midnight" has become one of cinema's best-known instructions.
Famous robots from movies and TV.Elmo: Elmo is a furry Sesame Street Muppet, not a robot. Performer Kevin Clash reshaped the character in the 1980s, turning a minor monster into a toddler favorite.

Software for recording and making music.GarageBand: Apple's free music app arrived in 2004 with the iLife suite, handing beginners virtual instruments and loops that once required a pricey studio.
Software for recording and making music.Logic Pro: Apple's pro-level studio, which started life as a German program named Notator, and it is widely used for scoring and pop production.
Software for recording and making music.Ableton Live: Built around a clip-launching view made for live performance, this Berlin-made program is a staple for electronic musicians and DJs.
Software for recording and making music.FL Studio: Once called FruityLoops, it started as a simple loop sequencer in 1997. Today many hip-hop and EDM producers build hits in it.
Software for recording and making music.Pro Tools: Since the 1990s it has been the industry-standard studio recorder, and a great number of the albums you've heard were mixed in it.
Software for recording and making music.Cubase: Steinberg's Cubase first appeared in 1989 and helped create the modern studio workflow, along with the VST plugin standard.
Software for recording and making music.Audacity: Free and open source since 2000, this editor is a go-to for podcasters and was built by volunteers from a Carnegie Mellon project.
Software for recording and making music.Reaper: Created by Winamp's co-creator Justin Frankel, this lightweight recorder is loved for its low price and endless customization.
Software for recording and making music.Bitwig: Founded by former Ableton engineers in Berlin, Bitwig Studio launched in 2014 and is known for flexible modular sound design.
Software for recording and making music.Photoshop: A trap: Adobe's image editor shapes pictures, not songs. Its name is so well known that it has become a verb for editing a photo.
Software for recording and making music.Premiere Pro: Adobe's video editor, used in feature films like Deadpool, can handle sound but is built for cutting footage rather than composing music.
Software for recording and making music.Final Cut Pro: Apple's video editor shares a maker with GarageBand, which is why it fits the question, but it edits video, not music.
Software for recording and making music.Excel: Spreadsheet software, so it doesn't fit, though musicians have sometimes tracked royalties and tour budgets in it. Launched for Mac in 1985.
Software for recording and making music.Blender: Free and open source, it makes 3D animation and visual effects. It can't record a song, though some of its short films have won awards.
Software for recording and making music.AutoCAD: Autodesk's design tool, first released in 1982, drafts buildings and machines, not music, and engineers have relied on it for decades.
Software for recording and making music.Spotify: Launched in 2008 in Sweden, it streams songs rather than making them. It's a place for listening, not for recording.
Software for recording and making music.Shazam: It identifies a song from a few seconds of audio. Apple bought it in 2018, but it recognizes music and can't create it.
Software for recording and making music.iTunes: Launched in 2001 to play and organize music, it changed how people bought songs, but it doesn't record or compose anything.
Software for recording and making music.Winamp: This 1997 media player, with its llama-themed slogan 'it really whips the llama's ass', plays music but can't make it.
Software for recording and making music.SoundCloud: A site where artists share tracks, a launchpad for many rappers, but the platform hosts music rather than helping you create it.
Software for recording and making music.Lightroom: Adobe's tool for photo editing and organizing. Despite sharing a brand with music apps' creator, it deals with images, not sound.
Software for recording and making music.Canva: Founded in Sydney in 2013, this design site makes posters and slides easy, but it has no tools for recording audio.
Software for recording and making music.Pandora: The Music Genome Project powers its radio-style recommendations, so it helps you discover tunes, not record your own.
Software for recording and making music.VLC: The traffic-cone media player plays almost any file format, so it's for listening and watching, and it won't help you record a track.

Novels by Stephen King.It: Published in 1986, this novel about Pennywise in Derry, Maine runs over 1,100 pages and took King years to write.
Novels by Stephen King.Carrie: King's first published novel, 1974; he threw the draft in the trash and his wife Tabitha pulled it back out.
Novels by Stephen King.The Shining: The Overlook Hotel was inspired by the Stanley Hotel in Colorado, and King famously disliked Kubrick's film.
Novels by Stephen King.Misery: Annie Wilkes, the 'number one fan' holding a novelist hostage, came from King's frustration with demanding fans and with his own addiction.
Novels by Stephen King.Cujo: The rabid St. Bernard terror of 1981; King has said he barely remembers writing it because of his drinking at the time.
Novels by Stephen King.Christine: A possessed 1958 Plymouth Fury terrorizes its owner; the novel was published in 1983.
Novels by Stephen King.Pet Sematary: King reportedly shelved it for a time because it disturbed him; the sign misspelling is the pet cemetery kids' own.
Novels by Stephen King.The Stand: A post-plague epic from 1978; the 1990 restored edition added roughly 400 pages cut from the original.
Novels by Stephen King.Salem's Lot: His 1975 vampire novel set in a Maine town; King said it was an homage to Dracula, which he read as a boy.
Novels by Stephen King.Dolores Claiborne: A 1992 novel told as one long monologue by a woman, without chapter breaks; it is a non-supernatural thriller.
Novels by Stephen King.The Green Mile: Originally published as six monthly paperbacks in 1996, like a Dickens serial, before appearing as one book.
Novels by Stephen King.Firestarter: A girl with the power to start fires is hunted by a secret agency in this 1980 novel.
Novels by Stephen King.Under the Dome: A 2009 novel of about 1,000 pages in which an invisible barrier suddenly seals a Maine town.
Novels by Stephen King.Doctor Sleep: The 2013 sequel to The Shining, following Danny Torrance as an adult, years after the Overlook Hotel.
Novels by Stephen King.Dracula: Bram Stoker's 1897 vampire novel, often confused with King's Salem's Lot; it was written in letters and diary entries.
Novels by Stephen King.Frankenstein: Mary Shelley's 1818 novel, begun when she was 18, which is not King's though it fits the horror theme.
Novels by Stephen King.Rebecca: Daphne du Maurier's 1938 novel opens with 'Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again.'
Novels by Stephen King.Jaws: Peter Benchley's 1974 shark novel, which Spielberg turned into the first summer blockbuster; not King's.
Novels by Stephen King.The Exorcist: William Peter Blatty's 1971 novel about demonic possession, adapted into the 1973 film; not by King.
Novels by Stephen King.Psycho: Robert Bloch's 1959 novel, made famous by Hitchcock's 1960 film; not a King book.
Novels by Stephen King.Coraline: Neil Gaiman's 2002 tale of a girl and her Other Mother, a creepy children's book not by King.
Novels by Stephen King.Rosemary's Baby: Ira Levin's 1967 novel set in a New York apartment building, a horror classic not by King.
Novels by Stephen King.Hannibal: Thomas Harris's 1999 sequel to The Silence of the Lambs, a thriller not by King.
Novels by Stephen King.Jurassic Park: Michael Crichton's 1990 novel about cloned dinosaurs, a thriller not by King.

Things in Macbeth.Witches: Three 'weird sisters' open the play by greeting Macbeth as future king; their chant 'Double, double toil and trouble' is among Shakespeare's best known.
Things in Macbeth.Cauldron: The witches' brew includes 'eye of newt and toe of frog', and the cauldron scene is where Macbeth gets his false-comfort prophecies.
Things in Macbeth.Dagger: Before murdering Duncan, Macbeth sees a floating dagger, which is a hallucination from a guilty mind.
Things in Macbeth.Ghost: Banquo's ghost appears at the feast, visible only to Macbeth, who panics in front of his guests.
Things in Macbeth.Crown: Macbeth seizes the Scottish crown by killing his king, though the witches had promised Banquo's heirs would rule.
Things in Macbeth.Birnam Wood: The prophecy says Macbeth is safe until the wood moves; soldiers carry branches as camouflage, so it appears to march on Dunsinane.
Things in Macbeth.Prophecy: The witches' predictions seem to guarantee Macbeth's rule, but each hides a loophole, such as one 'not born of woman'.
Things in Macbeth.Blood: Lady Macbeth's 'Out, damned spot!' is about imagined blood she cannot wash off, and it is among the play's central images.
Things in Macbeth.Castle: Macbeth's fortress at Dunsinane is where he is finally killed, and Inverness is where Duncan is murdered.
Things in Macbeth.Sleepwalking: Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and rubs her hands, revealing her guilt in a scene often cited in discussions of conscience.
Things in Macbeth.Thane: This Scottish noble title is what Macbeth is first called, Thane of Glamis, and then Cawdor.
Things in Macbeth.Apparitions: The witches conjure visions for Macbeth, including an armed head and a bloody child, each carrying a prophecy.
Things in Macbeth.Balcony: The balcony belongs to Romeo and Juliet, not the Scottish play.
Things in Macbeth.Skull: Yorick's skull is Hamlet's prop, not Macbeth's.
Things in Macbeth.Handkerchief: The fatal handkerchief is Othello's plot device.
Things in Macbeth.Shipwreck: Shipwrecks drive The Tempest and Twelfth Night, but not Macbeth.
Things in Macbeth.Pound of flesh: Shylock's pound of flesh is in The Merchant of Venice.
Things in Macbeth.Love potion: Love potions are in A Midsummer Night's Dream, and Macbeth has other potions only in the form of the witches' brew.
Things in Macbeth.Donkey's head: Bottom's donkey head is a comic gag from A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Things in Macbeth.Three caskets: The caskets are the suitors' test in The Merchant of Venice.
Things in Macbeth.Poisoned cup: The poisoned cup is how Hamlet ends, with Gertrude drinking from it; Macbeth has no such drink.
Things in Macbeth.Masquerade ball: The masked ball is in Romeo and Juliet, and Macbeth has only a banquet.
Things in Macbeth.Twins: Twins drive The Comedy of Errors and Twelfth Night, and not Macbeth.
Things in Macbeth.Island: The Tempest takes place on an island; Macbeth is set across Scotland.

Things smaller than a grain of rice.Bacterium: A typical bacterium is only about one to five micrometers long, so you could line up hundreds across a single rice grain.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Atom: An atom is about a tenth of a nanometer across, and a rice grain holds an enormous number of them, over a quintillion.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Dust mite: Dust mites measure around a third of a millimeter, invisible to the naked eye, and they feed on dead skin flakes.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Flea: Fleas are around two to three millimeters long, which is smaller than most rice grains, yet they can jump over a hundred times their body length.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Grain of sand: Sand grains are 0.06 to 2 millimeters, so most are smaller than a rice grain, and a handful has many thousands of them.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Pollen grain: A pollen grain is often only about 20 to 100 micrometers across, but under a microscope each plant's grain has a unique shape.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Red blood cell: A red blood cell is about 7 micrometers wide, and your body makes around two million of them every second.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Virus: Most viruses are about 20 to 300 nanometers long, far smaller than bacteria, and can only be seen with electron microscopes.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Poppy seed: Poppy seeds are about one millimeter across, and it takes around three million of them to make a single kilogram.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Salt crystal: A grain of table salt is a tiny cube, around 0.3 millimeters on a side, which is a shape set by sodium chloride's crystal lattice.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Mustard seed: A mustard seed is only a millimeter or two wide, but in the New Testament it stands as the symbol of something small that grows large.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Sesame seed: Sesame seeds are only about three millimeters long, and the pod splits open when ripe, which is often linked to the phrase 'open sesame'.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Amoeba: An amoeba is a single cell, often only a fraction of a millimeter, which moves by pushing out blobby arms called pseudopods.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Pea: A green pea is about 7 to 10 millimeters wide, well bigger than a grain of rice, and Gregor Mendel used them to discover genetics.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Coin: Even the smallest coins, like a US dime at 17.9 millimeters across, are much larger than a rice grain.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Marble: A standard marble is about 13 to 16 millimeters, and the larger ones, called shooters, can be an inch across.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Peanut: A peanut is not a nut, but a legume that ripens underground, and it is much larger than a rice grain.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Grape: A grape is roughly two centimeters, many times bigger than rice, and it is mostly water, around 80 percent.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Honeybee: A honeybee is around 12 to 15 millimeters long, bigger than a rice grain, and one makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her life.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Jellybean: The jellybean has a shell of sugar, is about two centimeters long, and is much bigger than rice.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Mouse: A house mouse weighs about 20 grams and is several centimeters long, so even a baby is far larger than a rice grain.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Paperclip: A standard paperclip is about 3 to 4 centimeters, making it many times longer than a rice grain.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Blueberry: Blueberries are around a centimeter across, and their frosty bloom is a natural wax coating, not dust.
Things smaller than a grain of rice.Acorn: An acorn is a few centimeters long, and an oak tree takes many years of growth before it begins to produce them.

Amusement park rides.Roller coaster: The first roller coasters were Russian ice slides, and Coney Island's 1884 Switchback Railway brought the idea to America at about 10 km/h.
Amusement park rides.Ferris wheel: George Ferris built the first giant wheel for the 1893 Chicago World's Fair to rival the Eiffel Tower.
Amusement park rides.Bumper cars: Bumper cars date to the 1920s and draw current from a metal ceiling through a pole, which keeps them moving without batteries.
Amusement park rides.Carousel: Carousel horses usually go around clockwise in Britain but counter-clockwise in the US, and the ride came from knights' jousting practice.
Amusement park rides.Log flume: A log flume rides hollow logs through a channel, and the final plunge soaks the front riders because the boat displaces water forward.
Amusement park rides.Teacups: The spinning Teacups ride at Disneyland was inspired by the Mad Hatter's tea party in Alice in Wonderland.
Amusement park rides.Ghost train: Ghost trains are dark rides in carts through spooky scenes, and the name remains common in Britain.
Amusement park rides.Drop tower: Drop towers lift riders high and release them in free fall, and some, such as Zumanjaro, drop over 100 meters.
Amusement park rides.Pirate ship: The pirate ship swings back and forth like a giant pendulum, and riders at the ends feel the strongest forces.
Amusement park rides.Waltzer: The Waltzer is a British fairground ride where cars spin on a rotating, wavy track, and operators spin them extra for thrills.
Amusement park rides.Helter skelter: The helter skelter is a spiral slide around a tower that riders descend on a mat, a fixture of British fairs since the Victorian era.
Amusement park rides.Seesaw: A seesaw is a playground lever, and it isn't a powered ride you'd find among amusement park attractions.
Amusement park rides.Monkey bars: Monkey bars are a playground climbing frame, and no ticket is needed since they're free and don't have a motor.
Amusement park rides.Sandbox: Sandboxes are play areas rather than rides, and children dig, build and pour in them without any motor.
Amusement park rides.Treadmill: Treadmills are gym machines, and the fun fair has no such item because they are used for exercise rather than thrills.
Amusement park rides.Escalator: Escalators are moving stairways, and the first was a fairground novelty in Coney Island, but it's not a ride today.
Amusement park rides.Moving walkway: Moving walkways in airports carry walkers at a gentle pace, and they weren't made for thrills.
Amusement park rides.Ski lift: Ski lifts carry people uphill to the slopes, and they feel like rides but serve transport rather than fun.
Amusement park rides.Zamboni: The Zamboni is an ice resurfacing machine, and it appears at hockey arenas rather than amusement parks.
Amusement park rides.Golf cart: Golf carts ferry players around a course, and electric ones are common at resorts, but they aren't a ride.
Amusement park rides.Revolving door: Revolving doors spin people through buildings and keep out drafts, and they were patented in 1888.
Amusement park rides.Hammock: Hammocks were invented by Central American peoples and spread to sailors, and they are for lazing rather than thrills.
Amusement park rides.Trampoline: The trampoline was named after the Spanish trampolin, and a bounce on one makes a good ride but not an amusement park standard.
Amusement park rides.Rocking chair: Rocking chairs soothe with a gentle sway and a slow rhythm, but they sit on porches and in living rooms, not on amusement park midways.

Real theme parks.Disneyland: Disneyland opened in Anaheim in 1955, and Walt Disney supposedly got the idea watching his daughters on a carousel.
Real theme parks.Universal Studios: Universal Studios in Hollywood began as a studio tour in 1964 and became a theme park attraction.
Real theme parks.Six Flags: Six Flags is named for the six flags that have flown over Texas, where the first park opened in 1961.
Real theme parks.Legoland: Legoland opened in Billund, Denmark, in 1968, and the original park is built from about 60 million Lego bricks.
Real theme parks.Alton Towers: Alton Towers in Staffordshire is Britain's biggest theme park, built around a ruined stately home.
Real theme parks.Busch Gardens: Busch Gardens began in Tampa as a free garden at a brewery, and grew into a theme park.
Real theme parks.Cedar Point: Cedar Point in Ohio is known as the 'Roller Coaster Capital of the World', with more than a dozen of them.
Real theme parks.Europa-Park: Europa-Park, in Germany, is the country's biggest theme park and is themed on European countries.
Real theme parks.Tivoli Gardens: Tivoli in Copenhagen opened in 1843, and it is among the oldest amusement parks in the world and a Disney inspiration.
Real theme parks.Dollywood: Dolly Parton's Tennessee park, near her hometown, mixes rides and Appalachian culture.
Real theme parks.Efteling: Efteling in the Netherlands opened in 1952 and is themed on fairy tales and fantasy.
Real theme parks.Central Park: Central Park in New York is a public park, designed by Olmsted and Vaux, with no rides beyond a carousel.
Real theme parks.Hyde Park: London's Hyde Park is a royal park known for Speakers' Corner, so it's a park, not a theme park.
Real theme parks.Yellowstone: Yellowstone, the first US national park, has geysers like Old Faithful, but no roller coasters.
Real theme parks.Jurassic Park: Jurassic Park is a fictional dinosaur theme park from the novel and film, and Universal does have a real ride based on it.
Real theme parks.Kew Gardens: Kew Gardens in London is a botanical garden with a huge collection of plants, not rides.
Real theme parks.Covent Garden: Covent Garden in London was a produce market, now a shopping and performance area, with no rides.
Real theme parks.Yosemite: Yosemite is a California national park known for El Capitan and its waterfalls, not a theme park.
Real theme parks.Fenway Park: Fenway Park is Boston's baseball stadium, not a theme park.
Real theme parks.Gorky Park: Moscow's Gorky Park is named for Maxim Gorky and has rides as well, but it's mostly a big public park.
Real theme parks.Park Güell: Park Güell in Barcelona is a Gaudí-designed public park with mosaics, not a theme park.
Real theme parks.Regent's Park: Regent's Park in London contains London Zoo, but it's a park, not a theme park.
Real theme parks.Hollywood Bowl: The Hollywood Bowl is an outdoor concert venue in Los Angeles, not a theme park.
Real theme parks.Battery Park: Battery Park is at the southern tip of Manhattan and is where ferries leave for the Statue of Liberty.

TV sitcoms (not dramas).Friends: The show's 1994 finale drew about 52 million US viewers, and the cast famously negotiated for equal salaries of a million dollars an episode.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Seinfeld: Billed as a show about nothing, it gave the world words like yada yada and Festivus; its finale in 1998 pulled in about 76 million viewers.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Frasier: This Cheers spin-off won a record five straight Emmys for best comedy series, from 1994 to 1998.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Cheers: Set in a Boston bar; its theme song says you want to go where everybody knows your name, and it ran for 11 seasons.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).The Office: The US version adapted the 2001 British original by Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant, and ran for nine seasons.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Community: A study group at a community college, with episodes spoofing everything from paintball to claymation; fans chanted six seasons and a movie.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Scrubs: Set in a hospital, it was praised by real doctors and nurses for realism, even in its absurd fantasies.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Fawlty Towers: With just twelve episodes, John Cleese's British hotel farce is regularly ranked among the greatest sitcoms ever.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Black Books: Dylan Moran plays a drunken, grumpy London bookshop owner in this cult British comedy.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Brooklyn Nine-Nine: NBC cancelled it after five seasons, but fans' outcry got it rescued within a day by another network.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Veep: Julia Louis-Dreyfus won six straight Emmys for playing Selina Meyer, a politician, in this Armando Iannucci-produced comedy.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Roseanne: This working-class family comedy returned in 2018 with huge ratings, before being cancelled quickly.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Breaking Bad: A drama, not a sitcom; it follows a chemistry teacher turned meth producer and is widely regarded as one of television's best.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).The Wire: A Baltimore crime drama and an HBO classic, often called among the greatest series ever.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Lost: A mystery-adventure drama about plane crash survivors on a mysterious island, with a famously argued finale.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).ER: A medical drama that ran for 15 seasons and launched George Clooney's career.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).House: A medical drama based loosely on Sherlock Holmes; House's name echoes Holmes and Dr Wilson is his Watson.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).The Sopranos: The mob drama of Tony Soprano; its cut-to-black ending is still debated.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Mad Men: A drama about 1960s advertising executives, famous for Don Draper and a fine eye for period detail.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Dexter: A crime drama about a forensic analyst who is also a vigilante serial killer.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Succession: A dark drama, with comic edges, about a media-empire family; it ended after four seasons.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Twin Peaks: David Lynch and Mark Frost's surreal murder mystery which asked who killed Laura Palmer; a drama, not a sitcom.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Fargo: An anthology crime drama inspired by the Coen Brothers' film; darkly funny but not a sitcom.
TV sitcoms (not dramas).Chernobyl: A 2019 HBO miniseries on the nuclear disaster, harrowing and the opposite of a sitcom.

Apollo 11 (not other missions).Neil Armstrong: The first person on the Moon, on July 20, 1969, spent roughly two and a half hours outside the lander.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Buzz Aldrin: The second man on the Moon; his MIT doctoral thesis was about orbital rendezvous.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Michael Collins: He orbited alone, out of radio contact whenever he passed behind the Moon, and later said he never felt lonely.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Columbia: The command module that carried the crew home is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Eagle: The lunar module landed with little fuel to spare after Armstrong steered past a boulder-filled crater.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Tranquility Base: Named in the first words from the surface: 'Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.'
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Giant leap: 'One giant leap for mankind'; Armstrong said he meant 'for a man', but the 'a' is hard to hear in the recording.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Sea of Tranquility: Mare Tranquillitatis is a dark basalt plain, named in the 1650s by Riccioli, not an actual sea.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).One small step: Armstrong's first words as he stepped off the ladder; hundreds of millions watched on television.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).July 1969: Launched July 16, landed July 20, and splashed down on July 24.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Gene Cernan: Apollo 17 commander, the last person to walk on the Moon, in December 1972, on a different mission.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Jim Lovell: Commander of Apollo 13, who also flew Apollo 8 around the Moon, but never landed on it.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).Alan Shepard: Apollo 14 commander who hit golf balls on the Moon; he was also the first American in space in 1961.
Apollo 11 (not other missions).John Glenn: First American to orbit Earth, in 1962; he flew again on a space shuttle at 77, but never to the Moon.

Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Suhoor: The pre-dawn meal before the fast; in many cities drummers walk the streets to wake people for it.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Iftar: The meal that breaks the fast at sunset, traditionally starting with dates and water.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Taraweeh: Special nightly prayers during Ramadan, in which many mosques recite the entire Quran over the month.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Laylat al-Qadr: The Night of Power, when the Quran was first revealed, believed to be better than a thousand months.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Sawm: Arabic for fasting, one of Islam's five pillars, from dawn to sunset throughout the month.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Fanous: A decorative lantern, especially in Egypt, where it has been a Ramadan symbol for centuries.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Hilal: The crescent moon whose sighting begins the month; Ramadan moves about 11 days earlier each year.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Ramadan Mubarak: A greeting meaning 'blessed Ramadan', exchanged among Muslims as the new month begins.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Zakat: Obligatory charity, a pillar of Islam that many give during Ramadan, often with Zakat al-Fitr at its end.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Imsak: The moment eating must stop before dawn; the word means 'abstaining'.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Lent: The Christian 40 days of fasting before Easter, so a different tradition from Ramadan.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Ash Wednesday: Begins Lent with ash crosses on the forehead, so it belongs to Christianity, not to Ramadan.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Yom Kippur: The Jewish Day of Atonement involves a 25-hour fast with no food or water, a different fast.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Tisha B'Av: A Jewish fast commemorating the destruction of the Temples, so not part of Ramadan.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Good Friday: A Christian day of fasting and mourning, so not a Ramadan term.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Advent: Four weeks before Christmas, a Christian time of preparation, not a Ramadan term.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Shrove Tuesday: The day before Lent when people use up eggs and fat, a Christian tradition.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Mardi Gras: French for 'Fat Tuesday', the last day of feasting before Lent, so not a Ramadan term.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Pancake Day: The British name for Shrove Tuesday, a pre-Lent day of eating pancakes, so not Ramadan.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Carnival: A pre-Lent party, possibly from 'carne vale', 'farewell to meat', so a Christian season, not Ramadan.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Maundy Thursday: A Holy Week day commemorating the Last Supper, so it belongs to Christianity, not Ramadan.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Hajj: The pilgrimage to Mecca is an Islamic duty but not part of Ramadan, held in another month.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Eid al-Adha: The Feast of Sacrifice marks the end of the Hajj, not Ramadan; Eid al-Fitr is the one that ends Ramadan.
Ramadan terms (not other fasts).Kol Nidre: The prayer that opens Yom Kippur, a Jewish ritual, so not a Ramadan term.
